title: Stochastic approximation with delayed updates: Asynchronous Machine Learning Algorithms study
abstract: In this paper, we investigate the convergence dynamics of stochastic approximation algorithms under delayed gradient updates and their impact on asynchronous machine learning performance. We present a comprehensive case study comparing the asymptotic behavior of stochastic gradient descent with theoretical guarantees from stochastic approximation theory, examining both decaying and constant learning rate regimes. For decaying rates, we verify convergence but demonstrate that high delays necessitate impractical learning rates; for constant rates, we show that systematically exploiting the learning rate and delay relationship enables robust asynchronous learning. Furthermore, we identify that popular adaptive optimizers degrade under delays because of estimating curvature at current rather than delayed iterates. Finally, we propose a theoretically grounded Hessian-based correction framework using modified Newton-Raphson iterations that explicitly account for gradient staleness.

title: Knowledge Graphs as External Memory for LLM-based Scientific Assistants
abstract: Scientific assistants must remember the questions, observations, parameters, and intermediate results that accumulate across days or weeks of inquiry, and trace each conclusion back to its evidence. Large Language Models (LLMs) lack such a structured, persistent memory, which causes contextual degradation, hallucinations, and excessive cost from overusing the context window. This thesis proposes a neuro-symbolic architecture that couples an LLM-based agent with a knowledge graph (KG) built on standardized formal languages (RDF, RDFS, OWL 2 RL, SHACL, SPARQL) and reusing existing ontologies (e.g. PROV-O) whenever possible. In contrast to state-of-the-art memory systems, which rely on schemaless or proprietary property graphs, our hypothesis is that grounding agent memory in open standards improves the six memory operations (consolidation, indexing, updating, forgetting, retrieval, compression) through formal reasoning and declarative validation, at a latency overhead that stays negligible relative to the LLM call. We present the problem, three research questions and their hypotheses, a first experimental prototype that implements an end-to-end store-and-retrieve pipeline, and an evaluation plan combining the LongMemEval and LoCoMo benchmarks with a test case in metabolomics.

title: LettRAGraph at LLMs4OL 2026 Task Flagship: Prompt-Guided Ontology Extraction with Ensembling
abstract: We present a system for constructing ontology graphs from text using openweight large language models. Our approach combines structured prompting, predicate normalization, and structural filtering. Prompt ablation experiments show that explicit taxonomy rules and closed-world constraints improve graph quality. We also introduce a conservative ensemble that retains only triples shared by two prompt configurations. On the official test set, the selected ensemble achieves Graph Similarity scores of 0.3584, 0.4872, and 0.5162 under exact, fuzzy, and semantic matching.

title: Towards Ontology-Guided and Traceable GraphRAG for Legal Knowledge in Industrial Maintenance
abstract: Regulatory industrial maintenance relies on legal texts that are numerous, evolving, and highly interconnected. GraphRAG extends Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) by integrating knowledge graphs (KGs) into retrieval and answer generation, offering a promising approach for exploiting the semantic relationships embedded in texts. However, current GraphRAG approaches using large language models (LLM) often rely on weakly constrained KG construction, lose explicit graph evidence during generation, and provide limited support for graph update under evolving corpora. This PhD proposal investigates GraphRAG as a knowledge engineering (KE) problem for legal knowledge management in industrial maintenance. The research focuses on three dimensions: (i) ontology-guided KG construction, (ii) evidence-preserving retrieval and generation, and (iii) evaluation of graph maintainability under evolving legal and regulatory corpora. Preliminary experiments on French legal corpora show that ontology guidance can reduce semantic noise and improve graph consistency, while underlining remaining challenges in relation normalisation and evidence traceability. Building on these results, we plan to design and evaluate methods for an ontology-guided and evidence-preserving GraphRAG pipeline evaluated through KG-level analysis, question answering performance, and human expert validation.

title: Automatically Building and Updating a Knowledge Graph of MLIP Models
abstract: Complementing the many efforts in providing semantic representations of concepts, notions, and entities in materials science, we report and illustrate a process by which we can automatically build a knowledge graph of the fast evolving field of machine learning applied to the prediction of material properties, focusing on MLIP (Machine Learning Interatomic Potential). This LLM-based process relies on multiple steps, from information extraction in documents and articles to a validation loop using SHACL constraints to detect and correct errors. It is carried out on a model-by-model basis, focusing on the consistency of representation, therefore enabling an iterative construction where the addition of new models is facilitated. We illustrate the process by showing a few interesting aspects that can be queried from a knowledge graph built from the models listed in the Matbench Discovery leaderboard.

title: The Agent Internet A New Evolutionary Phase of the Web and Its Global Impact
abstract: Large language model (LLM) based software agents are transitioning from one shot assistants to long term actors that plan, negotiate and accomplish tasks with multiple services. This transformation is resulting in what researchers call the Agent Internet, the Agentic Web or the Internet of Agents, in which programs are full-fledged players alongside people. This article summarizes academic surveys, industry studies and public market data from 2025 to 2026 to outline the multi-layered nature of this setup and to consider its pros and cons. According to market estimates, the revenue for agent software is estimated to be around eight billion dollars in 2025 and up to 35-53 billion dollars in 2030. Adoption statistics tell a tale of much experimentation and few pilots taking it to scale. We discuss communication protocols that enable agents to find and trust each other, the as yet undeveloped identity and payment layers and the burden of agent traffic on advertising supported content. But the challenges that we see are not just capabilities, but security, accountability, interoperability, and who pays for content and compute. Finally, we highlight some of the current research and policy gaps and suggest avenues for a responsible construction.

title: STAR-Q: A Web-Based Platform for Annotating Qualified Knowledge Graph Statements in Texts and Tables
abstract: The construction and evaluation of knowledge graph (KG) population systems depend on high-quality, entitygrounded annotated corpora. However, producing such corpora remains a laborious task: general-purpose annotation tools do not often support the grounding of annotations to KG identifiers, rarely handle tabular content, and provide little support for corpus-level quality control. In this paper, we present STAR-Q (Span and Table Annotation for RDF with Qualifiers), an open-source, web-based annotation platform designed to facilitate the annotation of both texts and tables with knowledge graph entities. STAR-Q lets users highlight mentions corresponding to subjects, predicates, objects, and ordered qualifier predicate-value pairs directly in documents, and then disambiguate them to entities and properties defined in a reference knowledge graph through a configurable lookup interface targeting any Wikibase instance. Wikidata is supported out of the box, with its large set of QIDs and PIDs. Private Wikibase deployments, such as enterprise knowledge graphs, can also be registered and selected per corpus. Annotations use a unified component schema covering both textual spans and character ranges within table cells; resolved values may be KG resources, corpus-local entities and relations, or typed literals. Beyond annotation, STAR-Q provides corpus management and import adapters for structured JSON/JSONL, archive-based corpus formats, Label Studio exports, and its own versioned full-corpus JSON. Annotations generated by the tool can be exported in RDF 1.2, either in a "truthy" statement mode or in a "full" mode preserving component-level text and table evidence using well-known ontologies (DCAT, PROV, NIF, CSVW, Web Annotations). Wikidata-grounded statements can additionally be exported as QuickStatements 3.0 commands for direct submission to Wikidata. We demonstrate STAR-Q through two scenarios: a didactic scenario based on Wookieepedia texts annotated with Wikidata entities curated by the WikiProject Star Wars community effort, and an industrial in-use scenario, where technical telecommunications documents are annotated against an enterprise knowledge graph. The tool is open source at https://github.com/ecladatta/star-q.

title: Modeling User Requirements for Inclusive Pedestrian Routing with the PIIRRITE Ontology.
abstract: Inclusive pedestrian routing requires not only a semantic description of the traversed environment and its dynamic contextual properties, but also expressive models of users' requirements. Existing ontology-based user profiling approaches primarily organize user characteristics into taxonomies, providing limited support for representing conditional requirements that can be evaluated against changing environmental properties. Conversely, ontologies describing pedestrian environments focus mainly on spatial and contextual information, with little support for modeling the structure and semantics of user requirements. This paper extends the PIIRRITE ontology with two new modelets for representing user requirements, including the accessibility-related ones, in pedestrian routing. Our model captures user profiles as sets of conditional requirements, distinguishes requirement importance from flexibility, supports recursively composed requirements, and introduces a distance factor mechanism for proximity-sensitive constraints. We validate the ontology by instantiating a knowledge graph of the LyonTech La Doua campus with representative user personas, evaluating SPARQL queries implementing a set of competency questions, and computing an inadequacy score quantifying a route's suitability for a given user profile.

title: Combining PageRank Modularization and Ontology Verbalization for LLM-Based Complex Ontology Matching
abstract: Complex matching remains a challenge in the ontology matching field. Existing approaches are constrained by strong assumptions on their input: instance-based and rule-mining systems require populated ontologies and reliable links between their instances, while systems built on pre-trained encoders operate at the schema level but target primarily simple correspondences. Recent approaches based on Large Language Models (LLMs) are promising, yet they either rely on manually built ontology modules or feed formal serializations directly to the model. This paper proposes a schema-only pipeline that addresses these limitations by integrating (i) an automatic modularization strategy combining the PageRank and Personalized PageRank algorithms, which reduces the search space while controlling the specificity of the extracted context; and (ii) a verbalization module that turns ontology modules into natural language descriptions, exploited both for embedding-based candidate generation and as context in LLM prompts. The approach is evaluated on four datasets of the OAEI Complex track. Relying solely on schema-level information, our matcher achieves competitive performance compared with state-of-the-art complex matching systems.

title: A Love Story in Patterns: Twenty years of ontology design patterns, continued with language models
abstract: Twenty years ago, a group of Semantic Web researchers set out to do for ontologies what the Gang of Four did for software. This talk retraces that love story, from NeOn and eXtreme Design to WOP, through an analysis of 788 papers. Language models now generate and match patterns, solving what we could not, while the bottleneck moves to trust. I argue that patterns matter more than ever, as the unit linking models, people and knowledge graphs, and outline the challenges ahead.

title: What WER Hides: A Closer Look at Algerian Code-Switched ASR
abstract: Automatic speech recognition for Algerian social-media speech is hard because of dialectal variation, Arabic-French code-switching, and non-standard orthography, yet these difficulties are usually summarised by a single word error rate that hides where recognition fails and whether gains reach information-bearing content. We evaluate seven systems on roughly 30 minutes of Algerian political social-media speech, annotated by language variety as Algerian dialect, Modern Standard Arabic, codeswitched, or French: a Whisper-large-v3 baseline, five Whisper variants fine-tuned on different combinations of broadcast, dialectal, and code-switched speech, and the prompted Qwen3-Omni model. The best system reduces overall WER from 60.1% to 31.3%, but still reaches 44.0% on code-switched speech, and named entities remain harder than ordinary tokens, with fewer than half preserved. These results show that ASR difficulty on Algerian social-media speech cannot be read from overall WER alone; it must be measured separately by language variety and by whether named entities survive.

title: Anomaly Detection using Source-Reversed Flow Matching
abstract: Anomaly detection in textual data remains an underexplored problem, hindered by fragmented benchmarks, scarce labeled data, and methods that fail to model the distribution of normal text in a continuous and generative manner. We propose FLOCAT 1 , an unsupervised approach that reformulates this task through a source-reversed flow matching paradigm: rather than learning to generate, we learn a flow from inlier text embeddings toward a lowvariance isotropic Gaussian target, whose radius is explicitly constrained to ensure that the distance to the centroid serves as a geometrically consistent anomaly score. Built on a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) backbone, FLO-CAT operates at both token and sentence level through a level-agnostic interpolation mechanism, enabling fine-grained signal interpretability. We evaluate on 10 datasets spanning text classification, spam detection, sentiment analysis, human-vs. machine-generated text and depression screening, consistently achieving state-of-the-art AUC-ROC across all benchmarks and text representations.

title: Are Benchmarks a source of bias in LLMs? MMLU, CommonSenseQA and MGSM under the Microscope
abstract: Evaluation is an essential process in the development and use of NLP systems. Benchmarks are widely used to calibrate systems, determine the efficiency of techniques, but also to advertise recently launched language models. Not only do benchmarks allow for evaluation and system comparisons, but they are also commonly utilized as training and validation corpora. In this paper, we aim at characterizing the "world knowledge" that is put forth by benchmarks by closely inspecting their content. Through qualitative manual annotations (+15k instances) as well as quantitative automatic analyses, we uncover the presence of both explicit and implicit biases in MMLU, Common-SenseQA and MGSM, ranging from representational imbalance to bluntly sexist and racist instances. Our findings demonstrate that current NLP evaluation practices pose numerous quality issues, reinforce stereotypes and even contain explicitly harmful content. The current operationalization of benchmarks is questioned, and we provide recommendations and directions for further ethical evaluation.

title: Sparse-station temperature interpolation via Gaussian-process committees: an artificial intelligence evaluation of variance-inflation risk in national heat-health alert triggering
abstract: Heat-health alert systems in data-sparse national settings depend on interpolated temperature fields whose uncertainty is rarely propagated into the trigger decision. The analysis treats a committee of local Gaussian-process experts as a weighted product-of-experts and derives the committee predictive variance as a quadratic form in the per-expert variances, with an inflation factor that grows with the disagreement between expert means and shrinks with the trace of the committee weight matrix. A decision-theoretic framework is then constructed in which the alert trigger is a threshold on the posterior mean and the variance inflation enters through the probability of correct triggering. Using NASA POWER monthly reanalysis for Harare over 2000-2023 (312 monthly observations, mean 18.914 C, standard deviation 3.107 C, warming trend 0.2001 C per decade), the paper shows that the observed interannual variability is of the same order as the inflation the committee architecture can introduce, so that trigger reliability is sensitive to committee design rather than to the interpolation bias alone. The contribution is a formal criterion for bounding committee-induced variance inflation in sparse-station interpolation and a demonstration that alert-trigger reliability should be evaluated against the inflation bound rather than against point-estimate accuracy.

title: Differentially private federated crop-yield benchmarking across sovereign agricultural registries: a privacy-utility frontier analysis for climate analytics competition policy
abstract: Sovereign agricultural registries hold the crop-yield records that climate-analytics competition policy needs, yet the same records are personal data whose release is constrained by national privacy law. The framework combines a federated Laplace and Gaussian mechanism with a stratified yield model, and derives the sensitivity of benchmark statistics to the number of participating registries and the per-registry clipping bound. The framework is illustrated with a reanalysis of NASA POWER monthly air-temperature reanalysis for Accra, Ghana (2000-2023, 312 monthly observations, mean 26.521 C, warming trend 0.1622 C per decade), which supplies the climate covariate that a yield benchmark would condition on. Competition policy for climate analytics should regulate the privacy-utility frontier directly, rather than mandating either data sharing or data localisation.

title: A Multimetric Evaluation of Ensemble and Neural Models for Imbalanced Credit Scoring on the German Credit Dataset
abstract: Credit scoring models must balance global discrimination, minority-class detection, probability quality, and computational efficiency, particularly when default cases are less frequent than non-default cases. This study benchmarks Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and a Multilayer Perceptron using the German Credit Dataset, which contains 1,000 borrower records. All models were evaluated using a consistent preprocessing, partitioning, and imbalance-aware training protocol. Performance was assessed through ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, Balanced Accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, Brier Score, and computational time. The results indicate moderate predictive performance across the evaluated models. XGBoost achieved the highest global discrimination with a ROC-AUC of 0.764, whereas the MLP obtained the highest PR-AUC of 0.378 and the lowest Brier Score of 0.123, indicating the best native probability quality among the evaluated models. No post-hoc probability calibration was applied. However, the MLP produced lower recall at the selected classification threshold. Logistic Regression required the least computation but recorded the lowest ROC-AUC and PR-AUC. Exploratory SHAP analysis was used to identify influential borrower attributes. These benchmark-specific findings demonstrate that model selection depends on the intended decision objective rather than architectural complexity alone.

title: An Uncertainty-Aware Hybrid Symbolic-Lexicon Framework for Multi-Domain Sentiment Classification
abstract: Multi-domain sentiment classifiers may return a polarity label even when the evidence behind that decision becomes fragile under domain shift. This study evaluates an uncertainty-aware hybrid symbolic-lexicon framework designed to pair each polarity prediction with a traceable accept-or-defer status. The framework combines a lexical branch adapted only on training data with training-only fitted symbolic feature states, variable-precision rough evidence, and nested score fusion. Evaluation uses the UCI Sentiment Labelled Sentences dataset, comprising 3,000 balanced English sentences from Amazon Cells, IMDb, and Yelp, under repeated within-source, pooled multi-domain, and leave-one-source-out protocols. In pooled evaluation, the framework achieved 83.73% accuracy and 83.76% F1-score, improving F1 by 0.50 points over the adaptive lexical branch. The boundary mechanism deferred 53.55% of cases and retained 92.54% accuracy among accepted predictions; however, matched-coverage logistic regression and SVM confidence rankings produced lower selective risk. The contribution is therefore a reproducible, algorithmically traceable polarity-and-deferment mechanism rather than a claim of universal predictive or uncertainty-ranking superiority.

title: Calibrated Is Not Informative: What a Fall in Expected Calibration Error Shows About LLM Confidence, Why Verbalised Scores Fail on Resolution as Well as Level, and the Recalibration Baseline the Ensembling Results Omit
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research A common finding in work on language-model confidence is that a model asked to state its own confidence in one pass is badly overconfident, and that some added procedure - sampling several answers, a separate critique pass, a longer chain of thought - repairs it. The repair is usually scored by expected calibration error (ECE). A 2026 telecommunications study is a clear recent case: it reports that averaging several blind self-evaluations of a reasoning chain cuts ECE by up to 88 percent on three telecom benchmarks, and it reports no discrimination metric. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that such claims mix two failures that need different fixes. One is level: the scores sit too high on average. The other is resolution: the scores barely separate right answers from wrong ones. ECE mostly measures level. It can reach zero for a constant score that separates nothing, and a monotone map fitted on held-out labels can remove most level error without changing the ranking at all. In the published studies that report both ECE and a ranking metric, the two move independently. Better prompts cut ECE while, in the authors' summary, AUROC stayed close to chance. Verbalised scores cut ECE on one benchmark by three quarters while the area under the selective accuracy curve rose by about one point. Sampling several answers raised AUROC from 54.8 to 92.7 on arithmetic but by one point on a yes-no reasoning set, and a separate self-evaluation pass, the mechanism the telecom method repeats, was at chance on the one multiple-choice set where it was measured alone. Re-reading the telecom study's own tables, the author finds that its top confidence tier was about three points more accurate than the pooled base rate, and that its largest ECE reduction comes from a 150-item subset, where binning noise alone is close to the reported post-method value. The paper gives a decision procedure and five tests that would separate what added inference passes buy from what a cheap recalibration already buys.

title: Comparative Machine Learning Bias Correction of Satellite-Derived Solar Irradiance at Tropical Stations in Central Java, Indonesia
abstract: Satellite-derived Global Horizontal Irradiance products carry systematic bias in tropical regions, so site-level correction is a prerequisite for their use where ground networks are sparse. This study compares bias-correction methods for NASA POWER daily irradiance in Central Java, Indonesia, and asks how much reported accuracy reflects algebraic dependence between predictors and the ground reference. Ten PUSDATARU stations were analysed over 2020–2024 (17,072 station-days; 8,459 from five exactly co-located stations). Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, Elastic Net, and Quantile Mapping were trained chronologically (2020–2022/2023/2024) against persistence and climatology baselines, with preprocessing fitted on training data only, paired significance tests, leave-one-station-out validation, and SHAP attribution. Random Forest reduced RMSE from 3.398 to 2.674 MJ m⁻² day⁻¹ (21.3%), lowered mean bias from 0.988 to 0.221, and raised R² from 0.266 to 0.546; across ten stations XGBoost reduced error from 5.921 to 2.831. Differences among tree ensembles were not statistically robust, and the weighted ensemble gave no gain at the highest inference cost. Adding ground-observed sunshine as a predictor raised the coefficient of determination to 0.9994, identified as recovery of the Ångström–Prescott expression defining the reference (70.9% attribution). Near-perfect accuracies against sunshine-derived references therefore measure leakage, not skill; correction also failed to transfer spatially, motivating sub-degree geostationary products as the next step.

title: Comparative Classification of DNS-over-HTTPS Traffic on the CIRACIC-DoHBrw-2020 Dataset Using Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost
abstract: DNS over HTTPS (DoH) improves the confidentiality of domain-name resolution but reduces the visibility available to enterprise monitoring and security systems because DNS is carried within encrypted HTTPS traffic. This study compares Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost for distinguishing DoH from non-DoH HTTPS traffic while examining predictive performance, computational cost, and model interpretability. The models were evaluated using the cleaned Layer 1 representation of the CIRA-CIC-DoHBrw-2020 dataset, which contains 1,019,117 flow records and 29 statistical predictors. The controlled protocol used three repeated 80:20 stratified development-test splits (seeds 42, 52, and 62), three-fold cross-validation, class-imbalance treatment, held-out testing, execution-time measurement, and permutation importance. Random Forest produced the strongest threshold-dependent results, achieving a macro F1 of 0.9965, MCC of 0.9930, and false-positive rate of 0.0011. XGBoost obtained the highest Average Precision (0.9994) and required a mean training time of 31.40 seconds, approximately 95.8% lower than Random Forest (743.42 seconds). Logistic Regression was computationally efficient but yielded lower DoH precision and a false-positive rate of 0.1197. PacketLengthMode was the most influential feature for both tree-based models. The results demonstrate strong within-benchmark separation, but they do not establish cross-network or operational generalisation.

title: Sparse Gaussian-process emulation of regional climate projections with active budget allocation: a computer-science evaluation of tail-quantile fidelity in adaptation screening
abstract: Sparse Gaussian-process emulators are increasingly proposed as surrogates for expensive regional climate model ensembles, but their fidelity in the distributional tails—where adaptation decisions are actually made—remains poorly characterised. The framework is evaluated on NASA POWER monthly reanalysis for Lagos, Nigeria (2000–2023, 312 observations), where the mean temperature was 26.414 °C and the warming trend was 0.1553 °C per decade. The analysis formalises tail-quantile risk as a weighted integrated quantile discrepancy, derives a variational lower bound that decomposes into a global fit term and a tail-sensitive term, and shows that uniform budget allocation is provably suboptimal under mild conditions on the tail weight. A greedy active-allocation algorithm is proposed and its submodularity established, yielding a (1−1/e) approximation guarantee. Tail-quantile fidelity should be treated as a first-class design objective in climate-emulator construction, and that active budget allocation offers a principled route to improving tail performance without increasing simulator cost. The contribution is a computer-science evaluation framework, not an empirical validation of any deployed emulator.

title: Adversarial-robustness certification of flood-susceptibility classifiers under projected land-cover regime shift: a computer-science evaluation of false-negative exposure in municipal zoning analytics
abstract: Flood-susceptibility classifiers used in municipal zoning are typically validated on historical land-cover distributions, yet zoning decisions bind future development under land-cover regimes that differ from those on which the classifiers were trained. the present analysis formalises the resulting certification problem as one of bounding the false-negative rate of a learned classifier under a projected covariate shift induced by land-cover regime change. A distributionally robust certification framework is developed in which the shift is represented by a Wasserstein ball around the empirical feature distribution, and a tractable upper bound on the false-negative rate is derived via a Lipschitz-continuous surrogate of the classifier's decision boundary. The bound is shown to be tight under a margin condition and to degrade gracefully as the radius of the shift ball grows. A case study using NASA POWER monthly reanalysis air temperature for Harare, Zimbabwe (2000–2023, 312 monthly observations, mean 18.914 °C, warming trend 0.2001 °C per decade) illustrates how a slow climatic drift can be encoded as a sequence of shift radii and how the certified false-negative bound responds. The analysis indicates that classifiers with high nominal accuracy can nonetheless carry substantial certified false-negative exposure under plausible land-cover projections, and that the exposure is concentrated in the decision-boundary region where zoning stakes are highest. The contribution is a certification procedure that municipal analytics teams can apply before deploying a susceptibility classifier under a projected regime shift, together with a formal characterisation of when such certification is informative and when it is vacuous.

title: Anexo - Python: Parte 3
abstract: Este capítulo serve como uma etapa preparatória para o estudo de estruturas bidimensionais e matrizes, focando na consolidação teórica e prática sobre listas unidimensionais (vetores) em Python. O texto destaca as características dinâmicas, ordenadas e mutáveis das listas, apresentando operações fundamentais como alocação por índices inteiros, adição de elementos com o método append, iteração de laços e medição do tamanho com a função len. Além disso, revisa conceitos como o uso de acumuladores para cálculo de soma e média, o produto escalar na álgebra linear computacional e propõe um conjunto de exercícios práticos que englobam leitura de dados, inversão de listas, busca de maior e menor valor com seus respectivos índices, separação de pares/ímpares e geração de vetores nulos para inicialização de linhas.

title: Graph-Enhanced Knowledge Tracing for Explainable Learner Modeling: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: Knowledge Tracing (KT) has become a central approach for modeling students' evolving knowledge states, but conventional sequence-based KT models offer limited representation of relationships among skills, concepts, and assessment indicators, reducing their interpretability for monitoring mastery and learning progression. This study systematically reviews how graph-based and knowledge graph-enhanced KT models have been developed, integrated, and evaluated to support skill mastery, learning outcome monitoring, and assessment-related interpretation. A PRISMA-based Systematic Literature Review was conducted using Scopus and IEEE Xplore, covering publications indexed from 2015 to 2025. From 116 initial records, 20 studies satisfied the eligibility criteria for active graph-enhanced KT and were included in the synthesis corpus, comprising 8 core (40.0%) and 12 supporting (60.0%) studies. Six major integration families were identified, including GCN/GNN-based, Knowledge Graph/ontology-enhanced, heterogeneous or multiplex graph, attention-over-graph, Q-matrix/concept map-based KT, and graph-supported recommendation. Graph-enhanced KT can enrich learner-state representation, support skill and mastery interpretation, and strengthen explainable learner modeling, particularly among core studies. However, active graph-KT integration remains limited, and issues of construct validity, cross-domain generalization, fairness, and deployment-oriented evaluation remain underexplored.

title: Federated learning for climate-model downscaling across data-scarce national meteorological services: a differential-privacy evaluation of forecast skill and sovereign data leakage
abstract: National meteorological services in data-scarce regions face a structural tension: statistical downscaling of coarse climate-model output requires large, pooled training corpora, yet the station records that would supply such corpora are sovereign assets whose transfer across borders is legally and politically constrained. Federated learning has been proposed as a resolution, but its privacy guarantees are usually asserted rather than quantified, and the trade-off between forecast skill and sovereign data leakage has not been formalised. The framework couples a formal leakage bound under (ε, δ)-differential privacy to a skill-degradation model for the downscaling task, and derives the conditions under which a federated, noise-perturbed ensemble retains useful forecast skill while bounding sovereign exposure. The privacy budget, not the federation topology, is the binding constraint on skill, and that the leakage bound is governed by the composition of local updates rather than by the number of participating services. The contribution is a formal, testable account of the skill–sovereignty frontier that national meteorological services can use to set privacy budgets before committing to federated infrastructure.

title: Differentially private computed generation of household energy-consumption microdata for urban heat-vulnerability mapping: a computer-science evaluation of equity-audit distortion under DP budgets
abstract: Differential privacy (DP) is increasingly proposed as the mechanism by which household energy microdata can be released for climate-analytics applications such as urban heat-vulnerability mapping, yet the distortion that DP noise introduces into equity audits of those data has not been characterised formally. It formalises the equity-audit statistic as a weighted function of household-level energy indicators and derives an upper bound on the sensitivity of that statistic to the replacement of a single household record, showing that the bound scales with the maximum household weight and with the range of the energy indicator. The bound is then propagated through the Gaussian and Laplace mechanisms to obtain closed-form expressions for the noise scale required to achieve a target (ε, δ)-guarantee, and the resulting mean-squared distortion of the audit statistic is expressed as a function of ε, the number of households, and the weight concentration. The analysis is anchored in the real DHS Program indicator 'Households possessing a computer' (HC_HEFF_H_CMP), which is used to characterise the empirical distribution of a household-level digital-access covariate across 27 African countries and 56 country-survey observations between 2015 and 2025 (mean 7.893, standard deviation 5.144, minimum Guinea 1.50, maximum South Africa 22.00).

title: Graph-matching domain adaptation for cross-border cropland masks: an artificial intelligence evaluation of label-scarcity transfer failure in national agricultural statistics
abstract: Cross-border transfer of cropland masks is routinely proposed as a remedy for label scarcity in national agricultural statistics, yet the conditions under which graph-matching domain adaptation fails have not been formalised. The analysis treats label scarcity as a structural property of the target domain rather than a sampling deficiency, and derives a bound on target risk that separates three additive components: graph-matching distortion, label-scarcity variance, and the divergence between source and target cropland definitions. The bound is used to identify a transfer-failure threshold below which adaptation is dominated by the unadapted source classifier. A formal proposition establishes that graph-matching distortion grows with the spectral gap between source and target adjacency structures, and a corollary shows that this distortion is not reduced by increasing the number of unlabelled target samples. The paper does not report empirical estimates; it provides the formal apparatus, the failure criterion, and the diagnostic quantities that a national statistical office would need to compute before adopting a transferred mask. The contribution is a specification of when cross-border graph-matching adaptation should be rejected, and a set of computable indicators that make that rejection auditable.

evidence.abstract: Cross-border transfer of cropland masks is routinely proposed as a remedy for label scarcity in national agricultural statistics, yet the conditions under which graph-matching domain adaptation fails have not been formalised. The analysis treats label scarcity as a structural property of the target domain rather than a sampling deficiency, and derives a bound on target risk that separates three additive components: graph-matching distortion, label-scarcity variance, and the divergence between source and target cropland definitions. The bound is used to identify a transfer-failure threshold below which adaptation is dominated by the unadapted source classifier. A formal proposition establishes that graph-matching distortion grows with the spectral gap between source and target adjacency structures, and a corollary shows that this distortion is not reduced by increasing the number of unlabelled target samples. The paper does not report empirical estimates; it provides the formal apparatus, the failure criterion, and the diagnostic quantities that a national statistical office would need to compute before adopting a transferred mask. The contribution is a specification of when cross-border graph-matching adaptation should be rejected, and a set of computable indicators that make that rejection auditable.

title: Multi-scale LSTM forecasting with attention-based feature fusion for anomaly detection in multivariate monitoring data
abstract: Abstract Engineering systems such as power equipment and industrial processes are monitored through multivariate time series whose anomalies appear at different temporal scales, from short fluctuations to deviations that persist over a whole operating cycle. A detector that reads a single input window has to commit to one of these scales. This paper presents MAF-LSTM, a forecasting-based anomaly detection framework in which parallel long short-term memory (LSTM) branches read input windows of different lengths, a scale-level attention module fuses their representations into a one-step-ahead forecast, and the forecasting residuals are scored with the Mahalanobis distance estimated on normal validation data. Experiments on smart meter data, two sets of high-voltage converter modulator pulses and a simulated chemical process show that MAF-LSTM achieves the highest AU-ROC and AU-PR of the five compared methods on all four datasets, exceeding the best baseline by 3.20 and 5.33 percentage points on average. An ablation study on the smart meter data quantifies the contribution of each component and shows that multi-scale modeling is most beneficial for anomalies with pronounced within-day fluctuation, where it matches or exceeds the best single-window model on each anomaly type without requiring the window length to be tuned.

title: Effects of Adversarial Training of Word Embeddings on Chinese Agricultural Pest and Disease Named Entity Recognition with BERT-CRF
abstract: Entity boundaries, confusable entity types and surface forms absent from the training data all make it harder to extract structured information from agricultural pest and disease texts. We examined whether single-step adversarial training of word embeddings with the fast gradient method (FGM) improves entity recognition when the BERT-CRF inference architecture is left unchanged. On the official 13-type AgCNER corpus, with exact matching of character span and entity type, we compared a feature-based CRF, BiLSTM-CRF, BERT-CRF and BERT-CRF+FGM, training each neural model with three fixed random seeds. BERT-CRF+FGM reached mean test precision, recall and F1 of 94.37%, 95.10% and 94.73%. Its F1 was 0.28 percentage points higher than that of the matched BERT-CRF baseline, and the paired difference was positive for every seed. F1 on unseen surface forms rose from 74.87% to 76.41%, and the overall gain remained 0.27 percentage points after test texts duplicated in other splits were removed. Mean F1 increased for 11 of the 13 types but fell for Company and Organization. FGM did not change the parameter count. The seed-42 model produced 20,670 indexed entity occurrences that can be checked against the released records and character spans. The official test set had been used in an earlier baseline study and test results informed model adoption, so these findings are exploratory; independently sourced data are needed to assess how far they generalize.

title: Federated learning of crop-disease classifiers across quarantine-silenced phytosanitary archives: a computer-science evaluation of privacy-utility trade-offs for cross-border outbreak analytics
abstract: Phytosanitary archives hold the labelled crop-disease observations that cross-border outbreak analytics require, yet quarantine regulation, commercial confidentiality and national data sovereignty keep those archives closed to centralised training. the present analysis formalises federated learning over such archives as a constrained optimisation problem in which each participating authority trains a local classifier on its own held-out data and shares only parameter updates under a differential-privacy mechanism. The framework is evaluated analytically rather than empirically: we derive a Rényi-differential-privacy accountant for the interleaved Gaussian mechanism, bound the generalisation gap of the federated averaged classifier as a function of archive heterogeneity and privacy budget, and characterise the privacy-utility frontier as a Pareto surface whose curvature is governed by the number of participating archives and the Dirichlet concentration of their label distributions. The analysis is illustrated with a reanalysis of NASA POWER MERRA-2 monthly air temperature for Kampala, Uganda (0.35° N, 32.58° E), 2000–2023, comprising 312 monthly observations with a mean of 22.443 °C and a linear warming trend of −0.1564 °C per decade, used here only to fix the climatic covariate distribution under which the classifier operates. The contribution is a decision procedure that lets a regional plant-protection organisation choose a privacy budget, an archive-participation set and a communication round count that together meet a stated outbreak-detection utility target without centralising any raw observation.

title: Hybrid IF–GNN–IF Framework for Suspected Fraud Detection in Bank Switching Transactions
abstract: Fraud detection in financial transactions remains a major challenge in the banking industry, particularly in bank switching systems that process high transaction volumes and involve complex interactions among transaction entities. This study proposes a hybrid Isolation Forest–Graph Neural Network–Isolation Forest (IF–GNN–IF) framework to identify suspected fraudulent transactions in bank switching data. In the first stage, Isolation Forest detects potentially anomalous transactions and produces anomaly scores that are used to construct pseudo-labels. In the second stage, a Graph Neural Network learns relational patterns from a transaction graph by integrating original transaction attributes with the pseudo-labels. In the final stage, the learned graph embeddings are combined with the original transaction features and evaluated using a second Isolation Forest to generate final anomaly scores. The framework was evaluated using 71,873 bank switching transaction records and achieved an accuracy of 0.9668, precision of 0.9200, recall of 0.3681, and an F1-score of 0.5258. The high precision indicates that the framework effectively identifies suspicious transaction patterns. However, the relatively low recall suggests that some suspected fraud cases remain undetected. Therefore, further validation using confirmed fraud labels is necessary to assess the practical effectiveness and generalizability of the proposed framework in real-world banking environments.

title: Enhanced Particle Swarm Sparrow Search Optimization for Aircraft Aerodynamic Parameter Identification
abstract: Abstract Accurate aerodynamic parameter identification is fundamental to achieving high-performance model‍-based aircraft control. To address the inherent challenges in this domain, this study introduces a novel hybrid optimization algorithm, the improved chaos particle swarm sparrow search algorithm (ICPSSSA), which synergistically combines the global search capabilities of the sparrow search algorithm (SSA) with the fine-tuning efficiency of particle swarm optimization (PSO). ICPSSSA enhances the optimization performance through three key innovations: the Kent chaotic map, which increases population diversity; an adaptive dynamic search mechanism, which balances exploration and exploitation, and the Lévy flight perturbation, which expands the global search radius. These components work in concert to accelerate convergence while avoiding local optima. By framing aerodynamic parameter identification as a nonlinear optimization problem, ICPSSSA was applied to both simulation scenarios and real flight data. The comparative results demonstrate that ICPSSSA consistently achieves superior accuracy, robustness, and convergence efficiency over conventional approaches, underscoring its promise as a powerful tool for high-fidelity aircraft modeling and control.

title: Evaluation of TF-IDF and Word2Vec Representations Using Support Vector Machine for Multiclass Product Category Classification of Tokopedia Reviews
abstract: As electronic commerce continues to expand, customer reviews have become an important source for automated text classification. This research evaluates and compares TF-IDF and Word2Vec representations for multiclass product category classification with Support Vector Machine (SVM). The experiment used the Tokopedia Product Reviews 2025 dataset containing 65,543 reviews across six product categories. After text preprocessing and keyword-based text refinement, 11,239 relevant reviews were retained. The dataset was divided into 80% training sets and 20% hold-out test sets. The reviews were transformed using TF-IDF and Word2Vec, while SMOTE was applied to the training data to handle the imbalance among product categories. Classification performance was assessed through five-fold cross-validation and a hold-out test set based on accuracy, macro precision, macro recall, and macro F1-score. Five-fold cross-validation showed that TF-IDF achieved mean accuracy, macro precision, macro recall, and macro F1-score of 95.95%, 93.13%, 92.78%, and 92.93%, respectively, compared with 90.80%, 84.58%, 86.02%, and 85.19% for Word2Vec. On the hold-out test set, TF-IDF achieved 95.42% accuracy and 91.88% macro F1-score, while Word2Vec achieved 91.01% and 84.91%, respectively. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test yielded a p-value of 0.0625, indicating no statistically significant difference at the 5% significance level. Nevertheless, TF-IDF consistently achieved higher descriptive performance than Word2Vec.

title: Deterministic reservoir computing for subseasonal rainfall forecasting under model-structure misspecification: a computer-science evaluation of forecast-value loss in rainfed advisory services
abstract: Subseasonal rainfall forecasts underpin rainfed agricultural advisories, yet the forecast systems that reach advisory services are typically evaluated on statistical accuracy rather than on the economic value of the decisions they inform. The central problem is model-structure misspecification: when the reservoir's assumed dynamical form departs from the generating process, forecast errors are not merely larger but differently structured, and the mapping from error structure to decision loss is nonlinear. The paper formalises forecast-value loss for a threshold-triggered advisory, derives a bound relating reservoir spectral radius and readout conditioning to the divergence between forecast-error and decision-loss orderings, and shows that two reservoirs with identical mean squared error can produce materially different advisory value. A methodological protocol is proposed for evaluating deterministic reservoir forecasters against decision-relevant criteria rather than accuracy alone. The contribution is a formal and methodological reframing of reservoir-computing evaluation for climate advisory services, with implications for how forecast value is reported to agricultural extension systems.

title: Anexo - Matrizes em Python
abstract: Este capítulo aborda os conceitos matemáticos e práticos de matrizes e sua implementação em Python, cobrindo desde as definições fundamentais de tipos (como matriz quadrada, identidade e nula), operações algébricas (adição, subtração, multiplicação por escalar, produto matricial) e cálculo de determinantes (pela regra 2x2 e Regra de Sarrus), até a manipulação direta de arquivos (txt e csv) através do comando with e do módulo csv. Além disso, o texto detalha a instalação e o uso das bibliotecas NumPy e Pandas, demonstrando na prática a criação de arranjos multidimensionais, a execução de cálculo matricial e a manipulação estruturada de dados tabulares utilizando DataFrames para leitura, seleção, filtragem e exportação.

title: Provenance-audited retrieval-augmented generation for national adaptation reporting: a computer-science evaluation of citation-fabrication risk in climate analytics pipelines
abstract: National adaptation reporting under the Paris Agreement requires climate-analytics pipelines that can trace every quantitative claim to a verifiable source. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) offers a way to ground narrative synthesis in a document corpus, but its citation behaviour under adversarial or sparse retrieval conditions remains uncharacterised. The framework defines a provenance graph over retrieved passages and generated claims, and introduces a fabrication-risk score that combines retrieval coverage, citation-claim entailment probability, and source-identity stability. A replication-based evaluation across 1,000 computed reporting tasks shows that fabrication risk rises sharply when retrieval coverage falls below 0.6 and when the corpus contains near-duplicate documents with conflicting metadata. The analysis identifies a coverage–fabrication trade-off that is invisible to standard RAG evaluation metrics such as answer accuracy or BLEU. The contribution is a formal, auditable risk model that national reporting teams can apply before deploying RAG in adaptation-pipeline workflows.

title: Federated Learning in the Wild: A Comparative Study for Cybersecurity under Non-IID and Unbalanced Settings
abstract: Machine Learning (ML) techniques have shown strong potential for network traffic analysis; however, their effectiveness depends on access to representative, up-to-date datasets, which is limited in cybersecurity due to privacy and data-sharing restrictions. To address this challenge, Federated Learning (FL) has recently emerged as a novel paradigm that enables collaborative training of ML models across multiple clients while ensuring that sensitive data remains local. Nevertheless, Federated Averaging (FedAvg), the canonical FL algorithm, has proven poor convergence in heterogeneous environments where data distributions are non-independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) and client datasets are unbalanced, conditions frequently observed in cybersecurity contexts. To overcome these challenges, several alternative FL strategies have been developed, yet their applicability to network intrusion detection remains insufficiently explored. This study systematically reviews and evaluates a range of FL methods in the context of intrusion detection for DDoS attacks. Using a dataset of network attacks within a Kubernetes-based testbed, we assess convergence efficiency, computational overhead, bandwidth consumption, and model accuracy. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comparative analysis of FL algorithms for intrusion detection under realistic non-i.i.d. and unbalanced settings, providing new insights for the design of robust, privacypreserving network security solutions.

title: Adversarial Machine Learning
abstract: Das Fachgebiet des Adversarial Machine Learning beschäftigt sich mit dem Auffinden von potenziellen Sicherheitslücken in Verfahren des maschinellen Lernens (ML) und der Entwicklung von geeigneten Gegenmaßnahmen diesbezüglich. So können beispielsweise manche ML-Verfahren durch subtile Veränderungen der Bildpunkte eines Bildes dazu veranlasst werden, anstatt des eigentlich dargestellten Objekts ein ganz anderes Objekt zu erkennen, obwohl das veränderte Bild für einen Menschen vom ursprünglichen Bild nicht zu unterscheiden ist. Bisher wurden ML-Verfahren dabei typischerweise nicht unter der Annahme entwickelt, dass sie in einer feindlichen Umgebung eingesetzt werden.

title: On the Simulation of Extreme Events with Neural Networks
abstract: This article aims at investigating the use of generative methods based on neural networks to simulate extreme events. Although very popular, these methods are mainly invoked in empirical works. Therefore, providing theoretical guidelines for using such models in extreme values context is of primal importance. To this end, we propose an overview of most recent generative methods dedicated to extremes, giving some theoretical and practical tips on their tail behaviour thanks to both extreme-value and copula tools.

title: On the adversarial robustness of spiking neural networks trained by local learning
abstract: Abstract Recent research has shown the vulnerability of Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) under adversarial examples that are nearly indistinguishable from clean data in the context of frame-based and event-based information. The majority of these studies are constrained in generating adversarial examples using Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT), a gradient-based method which lacks biological plausibility. In contrast, local learning methods, which relax many of BPTT's constraints, remain under-explored in the context of adversarial attacks. With the increasing real-world deployment of local learning methods in SNNs, it is critical to investigate whether these approaches introduce adversarial vulnerabilities that could compromise reliability. To address this problem, we examine adversarial robustness in SNNs through the framework of four types of training algorithms. We provide an in-depth analysis showing that direct gradient-based attacks are ineffective for locally trained models. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a hybrid adversarial attack paradigm that leverages the transferability of adversarial instances. The proposed hybrid approach demonstrates superior performance, outperforming existing adversarial attack methods. Furthermore, the generalizability of the method is assessed under multi-step adversarial attacks, adversarial attacks in black-box scenarios, and within the non-spiking domain.

title: Scalable architecture for measurement-induced squeezed light interferometers
abstract: Scalable interferometers lie at the heart of photonic quantum technologies, but their expansion has been fundamentally limited by optical losses that grow with circuit depth. Here, we introduce and experimentally demonstrate a measurement-induced architecture for multimode squeezed-light interferometers that overcomes this barrier. By shifting complexity from deep optical networks to programmable homodyne measurements, we realize effective transformations within a shallow, low-loss platform. We validate the principle with a six-mode device and extend it to a 400-mode interferometer, marking a leap in scale beyond conventional designs. Crucially, this strategy not only enables scalable squeezed light interferometry but also provides a powerful route to the generation of large-scale entangled states—a key requirement for quantum computing, simulation, and communication. Our results establish measurement-induced circuits as a practical pathway toward noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) applications and future demonstrations of quantum advantage.

title: Random purification channel made simple
abstract: The recently introduced random purification channel, which converts $n$ i.i.d. copies of any mixed quantum state into a uniform convex combination of $n$ i.i.d. copies of its purifications, has proved to be an extremely useful tool in quantum learning theory. Here we give a remarkably simple construction of this channel, making its known properties -- and several new ones -- immediately transparent. In particular, we show that the channel also purifies non-i.i.d. states: it transforms any permutationally symmetric state into a uniform convex combination of permutationally symmetric purifications, each differing only by a tensor-product unitary acting on the purifying system. We then apply the channel to give a one-line proof of (a stronger version of) the recently established Uhlmann's theorem for quantum divergences.

title: Ultrafast single-qubit gates through multi-photon transition removal
abstract: Abstract Fast qubit control is essential for scalable quantum computing. However, the strong driving that is required can induce significant leakage from the computational subspace, particularly in weakly anharmonic qubits. We demonstrate single qubit gates with a total leakage error consistently below 2.0 × 10 −5 on a transmon qubit, and obtain fidelities above 99.98% at 6.8 ns pulse duration in both X and X /2 gates. This is achieved by removing direct transitions beyond nearest-neighbor levels using double recursive applications of Derivative Removal by Adiabatic Gate pulse shape. We also introduce the amplified leakage error sequence which can directly measure the leakage error down to 10 −6 . We test single qubit gates across a range of pulse durations using multiple benchmarking methods to reveal the error channels. The presented approach can be straightforwardly adapted by other platforms.

title: Floquet-ADAPT-VQE: A Quantum Algorithm to Simulate Non-Equilibrium Physics in Periodically Driven Systems
abstract: Periodically driven quantum systems exhibit many fascinating phenomena absent in equilibrium systems, but their simulation is more challenging than that of static systems. Consequently, quantum simulation of these systems offers greater opportunity for achieving quantum advantage. To build the foundation for simulating time-periodic Hamiltonians, we utilize the Floquet-Hilbert space formalism to transform the Hamiltonian into a time-independent form and provide its Pauli decomposition. Within this formalism, we develop a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm, Floquet-ADAPT-VQE, that produces three key quantities that govern periodically driven quantum dynamics: the quasienergy, the associated Floquet eigenstates, and expectation values of observables with respect to these eigenstates. The latter is achieved by applying a fixed-depth quantum circuit to an initial Floquet eigenstate—an efficient construction made possible by the Floquet-Hilbert space formalism. We also identify a suitable auxiliary initial state whose squared Floquet energy is independent of the number of auxiliary qubits as well as the driving frequency, which leads to better convergence with fewer ADAPT iterations. We demonstrate our algorithm by performing numerical simulations on a periodically driven XYZ model with a magnetic field. We also explore potential applications of our algorithm for studying various non-equilibrium phenomena in periodically driven systems.

title: A new latent Dirichlet allocation for enhancing sentiment analysis in social network
abstract: The volume of sentiment-rich text data produced on a daily basis by social network sites such as Twitter is very large. However, traditional approaches to sentiment analysis, especially approaches based on the Bag-of-Words (BoW) model have a difficult time modeling more subtle thematic content structure and interrelationships in this data. The approaches tend to narrow down text to an easy word frequency level, leading to the loss of valuable semantic information required for accurate sentiment classification. This problem is even more evident when one has to work with large complex data. Furthermore, being high-dimensional feature spaces, BoW methods produce represented spaces that can saturate traditional classification models, decreasing their level of accuracy and reliability. The article overcomes these drawbacks of traditional topics modeling by considering using Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) as an intricate subject topic extraction method in English-language data tweets sentiment examination. LDA can reveal latent thematic structures in the tweets that enhance representation of features to be used in sentiment classification. The research methodology will consist of preprocessing the Twitter Sanders file, creating feature sets of different granularity (E40, E100, E300, E500), and testing them in Decision Trees (DT), Naive Bayes (NB) and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN). Such distinction of sets of features allows investigating the issue of influence of feature granularity on the performance of a classifier in more detail. Findings indicate that LDA-based features substantially outperform BoW-based features in sentiment classification across all evaluation metrics. Decision Tree and Naive Bayes classifiers achieved the highest accuracy, precision, and recall using LDA features, with optimal performance observed at the E300 configuration. KNN behaved better with the smaller feature sets and poorly with the larger features sets. These improvements have also been confirmed using statistical tests and this includes paired t-tests, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and are shown to be statistically significant across the board. These findings establish LDA as an effective and computationally efficient feature extraction technique for sentiment classification in social media data. This study contributes a systematic methodology for enhancing sentiment analysis accuracy and provides a foundation for future work integrating LDA with advanced machine learning algorithms.

title: Recurrent neural networks implemented through spatiotemporal light propagation in optical fibers
abstract: Recurrent neural networks excel at temporal tasks and video processing but require energy-intensive sequential memory operations. We demonstrate that multimode optical fibers naturally implement spatiotemporal recurrent computation through passive light propagation. Video frames are encoded onto separate optical beams with controlled time delays; these beams combine and recirculate through a fiber loop where interference and nonlinear propagation generate high-dimensional states encoding both current inputs and fading memory. Remarkably, the entire optical system remains fixed with no trainable parameters or electronic feedback, yet this single physical configuration achieves competitive performance across diverse temporal and spatiotemporal learning tasks: chaotic time-series forecasting, human action recognition, steering angle prediction, and surgical skill assessment. Our results show that recurrent temporal processing can emerge directly from spatiotemporal wave dynamics. This paradigm shift from algorithmic to physical recurrence offers an energy-efficient pathway to temporal artificial intelligence by leveraging intrinsic spatiotemporal optical nonlinearities within multimode fibers.

title: Comment on “Quantum limits to incoherent imaging are achieved by linear interferometry”
abstract: We show that the construction of the linear interferometer in the Supplemental Material of arXiv:1909.09581 is flawed, leading to a generally suboptimal solution. We then provide the correct derivation of the optimal interferometric configuration that achieves the quantum Fisher information limit for imaging N weak incoherent emitters.

title: Linear and cyclic codes over some special rings
abstract: The study of linear and cyclic codes over some types of finite rings has enabled the development of highly efficient codes with optimal parameters. Due to the algebraic properties of these rings, error-correction algorithms can be well adapted to diverse noisy channels, enhancing real-time performance. Furthermore, by using ideals in polynomial rings, cyclic codes ensure that hardware implementation remains remarkably straightforward and fast. For these reasons, in this paper, we describe linear and cyclic codes over the rings of the form $R_{s,p}= \mathbb{Z} _{p}[u]/\left( f\left( u\right) /\left( u-s\right) \right)$, where $p$ is a prime number and $f\left( u\right) = u^{p}-u$, with $s\in \{0,1,\dots,p-1\}$.

title: SpectralGuard: a Spectrally grounded λ-SHAP framework for XAI validity certification in pharmaceutical supply chain networks
abstract: Permutation-based explainability methods such as SHAP are central to regulatory compliance in AI-governed pharmaceutical supply chains across Sub-Saharan Africa, yet their validity depends on a structural property that existing frameworks do not monitor: the algebraic connectivity of the supply hypergraph, quantified by the Fiedler eigenvalue λ 2 . We prove that λ 2 → 0 is a sufficient condition for permutation-based XAI failure (Theorem 3.5): no increase in sampling effort can recover validity once network connectivity collapses. We introduce SpectralGuard, demonstrated on a calibrated synthetic DGP driven by real Eskom load-shedding and SARB ZAR/USD records ( n = 3, 227 business days, 2014–2026); all spectral results are from the synthetic hypergraph. λ-SHAP shrinks attributions toward a fluid-regime prior using λ 2 ( t ) as the shrinkage weight, maintaining auditability at an explicit bias–variance cost (Remark 3.12). A probabilistic validity certificate V ( t ) combines four spectral metrics with SHA-256 tamper-evidence. An oracle experiment ( B = 500, Seed = 2,026) demonstrates 70.4–89.2% attribution MSE reduction across governance regimes. The spectral gate is the decisive ablation component. In the synthetic DGP, early-warning detection leads classical baselines by 19 business days (λ c alert preceding the λ m crossing). Field validation on real CCMDD procurement data is planned for 2027 (PLMIF-2). A nine-step DHIS2 integration pathway supports SDG 3, 9, 13, and 16.

title: Lie Algebra-Based Quantum Optimal Controls Interpolation
abstract: Abstract We present a framework combining Lie group theory and feed-forward neural networks to efficiently generate quantum optimal control pulses for arbitrary unitary operations in superconducting qubit systems, bypassing the need for explicit optimization at inference time. The exponential scaling of the Hilbert space dimension with qubit number makes standard optimization approaches computationally prohibitive when large ensembles of distinct propagators must be processed, a bottleneck that is particularly acute in Trotterized quantum simulation. Our method addresses this limitation by pre-computing a representative set of control pulses via Lie group theory and training neural networks to map target propagators to their corresponding pulses. We demonstrate the approach on superconducting qubit systems of 2, 3, and 4 qubits, finding high reconstruction fidelity for specific combinations of Lie algebra parameters. As a physically motivated benchmark, we apply the methodology to reconstruct control pulses for the Trotter propagators of a neutrino system undergoing collective flavor oscillations. The successful generalization across system types demonstrates that a single model -trained once on hardware-specific random propagators -can serve as a universal control-pulse generator for any target quantum system of compatible Hilbert space dimension, offering a promising route toward scalable quantum simulation.

title: Optimizing Entanglement Distillation Policies via Markov Decision Process Formulation
abstract: Abstract Entanglement distillation is a fundamental operation in quantum information processing used to obtain higher-fidelity entangled pairs from a supply of less entangled quantum states using local operations aided by classical communication (LOCC). In a physically relevant setting, where states with an initial fidelity of f 0 , probabilistically generated over multiple, m, memory pairs distributed between two parties, Alice and Bob, are pairwise distilled, the optimal policy identifies the system configuration dependent sequence of entanglement generation and distillation operations that need to be performed in order to minimize the expected time to reach some target fidelity f T > f 0 . Here, we formulate and systematically analyze this task as a Markov decision process and using a value iteration algorithm, obtain optimal deterministic policies that minimize the expected waiting time required to achieve a target fidelity. Our results show that the expected waiting time under the optimal policy decreases with increasing generation probability p and number of quantum memories m -as expected. In contrast, it exhibits non-monotonic behavior with respect to f 0 for a fixed fidelity gap, (∆f = f T - f 0 ). While the optimal policy consistently outperforms baseline policies such as the greedy, nested and entanglement pumping policies, its relative advantage is regime-dependent, being determined by the system parameters (p, f 0 , f T , m), and exhibits a nontrivial dependence on the fidelity gap ∆f . Our results highlight the value of formulating entanglement distillation as a Markov decision problem, enabling the systematic design of policies that achieve target fidelity thresholds for quantum information tasks in realistic resource-constrained settings.

title: Sparse positive maps on qutrits with exact nondecomposability thresholds and PPT-entanglement transitions
abstract: Abstract We study a family of sparse positive maps on qutrits for which positivity, decomposability, and PPT entanglement can all be analysed explicitly. The block structure of the associated Choi matrices reduces positivity to a Hermitian biquadratic form and leads to exact positivity boundaries for three representative parametric families. For the same families we determine the exact transition between decomposable and non-decomposable maps and construct associated PPT states of two classes. The first consists of witness-adapted deformations naturally tied to the non-decomposability analysis. The second consists of analytically tractable families whose full PPT-entangled branch is detected by fixed positive maps, yielding exact thresholds between separability and bound entanglement. For the trace-preserving subclass, we further compare positivity with a recent eigenvalue bound for 2-positive maps, thereby making the gap between positivity and higher-order positivity fully explicit within this family.

title: LAMMPS-GUI: A Cross-Platform Graphical Tool to Learn and Explore Molecular Dynamics with LAMMPS
abstract: LAMMPS-GUI is a cross-platform Qt-based graphical application for the LAMMPS molecular dynamics simulation software. It integrates an input-script editor, live simulation execution via the LAMMPS C-library interface, log and thermodynamic-data viewing, interactive plotting, and snapshot/slide-show visualization into a single tool aimed at learning and exploring molecular dynamics with LAMMPS.

title: Quantum Imaging via Kurtosis-Difference Weighted Covariance on a 2D Camera
abstract: Abstract Camera-based quantum imaging detects spatially correlated photon pairs from spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC). Conventional covariance methods typically require tens of thousands of frames to extract weak correlations from noise. While thick crystals can increase photon flux, they generate photon pairs from multiple emission positions within the crystal, producing multiple correlation centers with complex pairing geometries. In addition, conventional covariance methods assume a single preselected correlation center and cannot fully exploit these distributed correlations. We demonstrate that kurtosis difference, a fourth-order statistic measuring tail similarity, effectively discriminates correlated pixel pairs even when correlation coefficients remain low. Weighting covariance by an exponential function of absolute kurtosis difference can select symmetric pixels while preserving true coincidences. This kurtosis weighting automatically identifies correlated pairs within a broad search region and accommodates multiple pairing geometries without requiring precise correlation center calibration. At 5000 frames, our method yields a contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) exceeding 7, whereas standard covariance remains below 2. Compared with standard covariance, the method reduces the acquisition time by 40-fold and could enable practical quantum imaging in sparse correlated-photon regimes.

title: Cross-Site Physics-Informed Transfer Learning for One-Hour-Ahead Photovoltaic Power Forecasting
abstract: Accurate short-term photovoltaic power forecasting is essential for grid scheduling, reserve allocation, and the reliable integration of renewable energy into power systems. However, many data-driven forecasting models are trained and evaluated at a single photovoltaic plant, which limits their transferability to plants operating under different climatic, geographic, and engineering conditions. This study evaluated a cross-site physics-informed transfer-learning framework for one-hour-ahead photovoltaic power forecasting across six heterogeneous solar plants. The framework integrated a hybrid temporal model with plant-level static descriptors and a physics-based power prior derived from irradiance, module temperature, installed capacity, and grid export limits. The primary experiment used six leave-one-site-out target folds: for each held-out target plant, the other five plants were pooled as the source domain for pretraining. A separate ordered single-source-to-single-target analysis (30 routes) was used only to examine pairwise source-target distance and route-dependent transfer behavior. Source-domain and target-domain validation data were kept separate during checkpoint selection. Compared with direct transfer and conventional fine-tuning in the primary held-out-target analysis, the full physics-informed transfer model reduced forecasting error across the evaluated target sites. The study provides a structured framework for cross-site photovoltaic forecasting under heterogeneous environmental and operational conditions.

title: GeoRacoon: A Python package for scalable, parallelized geospatial raster analysis
abstract: GeoRacoon is aimed at supporting work and analyses with large spatial raster data. It heavily relies on RasterIO (rio) extending its functionality and usability. Leveraging GDAL's block-based read/write capability, GeoRacoon implements efficient multi-core support (i.e. parallelization) for various high and low-level operations, such as convolution operations (e.g., applying a Gaussian filter) or even area-wide multiple linear regressions. It also facilitates GeoTIFF handling with an object oriented abstraction layer to RasterIO which incorporates the management of metadata with source and band tagging. GeoRacoon provides 3 packages, riogrande, convster, coonfit, which facilitate (in our opinion) working with TIFF files. evidence.title: GeoRacoon: A Python package for scalable, parallelized geospatial raster analysis

title: A Zero-Knowledge Backend Architecture for Preventing Data Leakage Using Hashing and Encryption
abstract: Backend services commonly receive, store, search, and analyze sensitive information in plaintext, creating exposure risks in databases, logs, caches, and application memory. This paper presents a zero-knowledge backend architecture that combines client-side data protection, protected search tokens, access-policy checks, and selected arithmetic over ciphertext representations. A lightweight Node.js prototype uses built-in modules only and demonstrates protected user-record storage, prefix-token search, and limited encrypted arithmetic. In the supplied experiment, username search took 0.077063 ms and encrypted aggregation took 0.035841 ms; statistics decryption took 20.696818 ms. These are prototype measurements, not general performance guarantees. The design reduces direct plaintext storage but is not a complete zero-knowledge system or production-ready cryptographic implementation. In particular, deriving a key directly from a predictable user identifier is insecure for production use, and protected indexes leak search structure. The contribution is an integrated architecture and a clearly scoped prototype evaluation for processing selected data without first decrypting stored values on the backend.

title: Donsker-Varadhan policy matching for reward-free offline reinforcement learning
abstract: This thesis studies an alternative method for reward-free offline reinforcement learning, investigating how well an agent can learn from a fixed dataset when reward guidance is missing, weak, or unreliable. A common way to handle this problem is behavior regularization, where the learned policy is kept close to the behavior policy that generated the dataset. This thesis studies an actor-to-behavior KL version of this idea using the Donsker–Varadhan representation of KL divergence. In contrast to behavior cloning’s behavior-to-actor KL direction, this actor-to-behavior direction can avoid the action-averaging problem. A reward-augmented alternative is also studied and can be used in settings where reward labeling is meaningful. In controlled settings, our method can recover KL divergence. However, its practical performance depends strongly on witness quality, optimization stability, and dataset structure. Therefore, while the method provides a principled framework for reward-free policy optimization, it does not consistently outperform established benchmark algorithms.
