title: Distributed Phase Tags: A Locality-Preserving Realification Compiler for Misty-State Quantum Programs
abstract: Complex amplitudes can be simulated over real Hilbert spaces by adjoining a two-dimensional real/imaginary degree of freedom. In a multipartite program, however, one globally shared phase tag is not a locality-preserving program transformation: every party would have to act on the same auxiliary system. We recast the distributed real simulation of multipartite quantum mechanics as a syntax-directed compiler into a real misty-state intermediate language. For $n$ parties we give explicit phase-reference codewords $\ket{0}_{P_n}$ and $\ket{1}_{P_n}$ on $n$ local tags and prove that the same real operator $J=XZ$ on any single tag realizes the logical action of multiplication by $i$. If a complex party-local gate is $A=A_R+iA_I$, its real translation is \[ \widehat A_j=A_R\otimes I+A_I\otimes J_j, \] which acts only on party $j$'s data and local phase tag. We prove an intertwining theorem for arbitrary finite party-local pure-state circuits, exact preservation of computational-basis measurement probabilities, preservation of the run-time interaction graph, and one-rebit-per-party overhead. For the canonical three-party GHZ program, the translation lies entirely inside the ordinary black-and-white misty gate fragment: controlled-$J$ replaces the complex phase operation, while the invariant $J_jJ_k\ket{0}_P=-\ket{0}_P$ transfers the required branch sign. This yields a short correctness proof for all four promised GHZ inputs and explains the earlier 64-path cancellation calculation at a single logical phase-code boundary. We distinguish this program realification problem from the weaker task of finding any real strategy with the same correlations, and state precisely which parts are known real-Hilbert-space simulation and which parts belong to the misty-language compilation layer developed here.

title: On the Adaptive Covering Complexity of Strings: Unifying Relative and Self-Referential Compression
abstract: We introduce and study the adaptive covering complexity C adapt S (s), defined as the minimum number of contiguous factor blocks required to partition a string s when each block is either a factor of a fixed external dictionary S or a factor of the target's already decoded prefix. This hybrid admissibility model formalizes the structural interaction between static dictionary matching and dynamic nonoverlapping self-referencing. Our main theoretical result is the exact logarithmic law which is tight and proves that dynamic self-reference can reduce phrase count by at most an exponential factor over static dictionary covering alone. We establish structural equivalences showing that the measure bridges word-segmented Relative Lempel-Ziv and non-overlapping LZ77, and we prove exact preset-history LZ77 sandwich bounds. Furthermore, we establish the optimality of the longest-match greedy parse via an exchange lemma and present an optimal implementation based on dual suffix automata running in O(M + n) time and space for a constant alphabet. These analytical results are complemented by counting bounds, stationary-ergodic asymptotic invariance, a dictionaryselection NP-hardness result, and a concise empirical illustration.

title: Tetrahedral Compression Minimax E3: Exact SOS Certificate and Verification Code
abstract: This archive contains the exact algebraic sum-of-squares (SOS) certificate and reproducible verification code for the universal tetrahedral quantum compression inequality associated with the P014 research manuscript, Sharp Completeness Thresholds and Reservoir Costs Across Temperature Regimes. The software verifies 356 algebraic SOS coefficient equations, the strict positivity of seven Gram blocks, rigorous rational bounds for 353 pivot variables, and the exact optimality of the symmetric-square 2-to-3 quantum compression construction. The archive includes a FLINT-independent exact verification procedure, an independent arithmetic reconstruction sharing the original symbolic moment rules, and supplementary physical consistency checks for energy-preserving thermal operations. The principal result is the sharp tetrahedral minimax constant g = (3 − 2√2)/3. This release is permanently associated with GitHub tag v0.1.1 and commit 17e1d5e99d4a03fd44da1f8f44609ff4494a7d54. The code and documentation are distributed under BSD-3-Clause, while the designated mathematical certificate datasets are distributed under CC0 1.0. The unpublished manuscript and internal scientific review material are not included.

title: ESTIMATING DAILY SOLAR IRRADIATION FROM SUNSHINE DURATION ACROSS THE SAHARA–SAHEL GRADIENT OF NIGER: AN ÅNGSTRÖM–PRESCOTT SCENARIO ASSESSMENT
abstract: Ground-based irradiance measurements are almost absent in Niger, so photovoltaic (PV) planning relies on satellite or reanalysis products or on sunshine-duration proxies. This study estimates daily global horizontal irradiation (Rs) from ten years (2015–2024) of daily sunshine-duration records at three synoptic stations spanning the Sahara–Sahel gradient (Bilma, Agadez Aéro and N’Guigmi), using the Ångström–Prescott model applied at daily resolution with generic coefficients (a = 0.25, b = 0.50). A documented quality-control pass resolved duplicated monthly records, excluded values entered under non-existent dates and capped five marginal cases in which sunshine duration exceeded the astronomical day length. Coefficient uncertainty was represented by a scenario envelope (a = 0.20–0.30, b = 0.40–0.60) rather than a statistical interval. The central annual mean Rs was 5.57, 5.99 and 6.03 kWh m−2 d−1 at Agadez, Bilma and N’Guigmi, respectively. Monthly climatological means ranged from 4.64 to 6.61 kWh m−2 d−1, whereas the coefficient scenarios shifted the annual means between 4.46 and 7.24 kWh m−2 d−1. The June–August minimum of sunshine fraction was negatively associated with maximum relative humidity at Agadez (r = −0.53) and N’Guigmi (r = −0.69) but not at Bilma (r = +0.20), suggesting a different control at the Saharan station. The clearness index is shown to be an algebraic rescaling of the same input and is reported only as a diagnostic. The estimates are internally consistent but uncalibrated and unvalidated; a validation protocol against satellite and reanalysis products is specified.

title: Tutores de IA: desempeño asistido, aprendizaje autónomo y transferencia / AI tutors: assisted performance, unaided learning and transfer
abstract: El desempeño obtenido mientras un tutor generativo está disponible no permite identificar, por sí solo, lo que el estudiante podrá hacer después sin ayuda. Este artículo examina una selección de experimentos de educación secundaria y superior, herramientas que asisten a estudiantes o a tutores humanos, y documentos de adopción y orientación institucional. La síntesis distingue práctica asistida, prueba autónoma inmediata, retención diferida, transferencia y evaluación del curso, y registra para cada estudio el diseño (ensayo aleatorizado individual, por aula o cruzado; laboratorio o campo), la población y la métrica del efecto. En el mismo ensayo de matemáticas de secundaria, el acceso sin barreras mejora la práctica y empeora el examen sin recursos. Otros ensayos encuentran mejoras autónomas con acceso continuo a un tutor de lectura o una semana después de estudiar con IA de propósito general, y otros aún encuentran beneficios próximos sin mejora detectada al final del curso o efectos pequeños, similares a los de la práctica sin tutor. Esa heterogeneidad no respalda ni una tesis de daño universal ni una de beneficio inherente al acceso. Se propone una ficha de comparabilidad que conserva intervención, comparador, población, unidad de asignación, momento, disponibilidad de ayuda y estimando, y un protocolo de aceptación que separa eficacia, implementación, acceso y coste; ambos son elaboración propia sin validación empírica. No se calcula un efecto medio ni se presentan experimentos nuevos. La conclusión es exigir evidencia adecuada a la capacidad que se desea desarrollar, sin convertir una nota asistida, una encuesta de uso o una conversión a años equivalentes en un desenlace que no se observó. English abstract: Performance achieved while a generative tutor is available does not, by itself, identify what a learner will be able to do later without assistance. This scoped critical synthesis examines selected secondary and higher education experiments, systems supporting learners or human tutors, and adoption and institutional guidance documents. It distinguishes assisted practice, immediate unaided assessment, delayed retention, transfer and course-level outcomes, and records each study's design (individual, classroom-level or crossover randomised trial; laboratory or field), population and effect metric. Within one secondary mathematics trial, unrestricted access improves practice and worsens the unaided exam. Other trials find unaided gains with continuous access to a reading tutor or one week after studying with general-purpose AI, and others find proximal benefits without a detected end-of-course improvement, or small effects similar to practice without the tutor. This heterogeneity supports neither universal harm nor an inherent benefit of access. We propose a comparability record preserving the intervention, comparator, population, assignment unit, timing, assistance availability and estimand, and an acceptance protocol separating effectiveness, implementation, access and cost; both are the author's proposals without empirical validation. No pooled effect or new experimental result is reported. Evidence should match the capability an intervention is intended to develop; assisted scores, usage surveys and conversions into equivalent years must not replace outcomes that were not observed. Working paper de la serie WHITE-PAPERS (wp-2026-029, v0.9). Incluye versión en español e inglés. No revisado por pares. Uso de herramientas de IA declarado en el manuscrito; sin conflictos de interés ni financiación.

title: SecondThought: Confidence-Gated Reasoning for Tool Calls in Small Local Models (code and results)
abstract: Reads a tool call's own token log-probabilities to decide when a small model should think before calling a tool. Thinking on the least confident 30% of requests keeps most of the gain of always thinking at about half the output tokens, and avoids thinking's tendency to call tools when none fit. Includes code, all responses on BFCL with Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B, and the paper.

title: A COMPARATIVE STUDY OF MACHINE LEARNING TECHNIQUES FOR REAL-TIME SENTIMENT ANALYSIS USING WEB SCRAPING
abstract: Real-time sentiment analysis is an important task for understanding public opinions, emotions, and attitudes expressed through online content. This study presents a machine learning-based Real-Time Sentiment Analysis System with Web Scraping to classify textual data into positive and negative sentiments. The proposed system uses the Sentiment140 dataset, which contains Twitter messages labelled according to their sentiment polarity, for training and evaluating classification models. Three machine learning algorithms, namely Naïve Bayes, Linear Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) Classifier, are considered for comparative evaluation. The methodology involves text preprocessing, removal of unnecessary characters and URLs, transformation of textual data into numerical features using Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF), model training, sentiment prediction, and performance evaluation. Web scraping is incorporated to collect relevant textual content from online sources for sentiment analysis, where applicable. The performance of the models is evaluated using metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and confusion matrix to understand their classification capabilities. The experimental results obtained for the Linear SVM and SGD models show accuracies of 80.49% and 77.60%, respectively, under their respective experimental settings. The proposed system provides a framework for analyzing online text and identifying positive and negative opinions efficiently. This approach can support applications such as product review analysis, social media opinion monitoring, and customer feedback analysis. The comparative study highlights the applicability of machine learning techniques in sentiment classification and provides a basis for selecting suitable models for real-time sentiment analysis applications.

title: Artifact: per-process RNDR/RNDRRS interception for record and replay on Arm
abstract: Research-side components behind the CSET 2026 paper "Three Months to Flip One Bit: Upstreaming Replay Support for Hardware Entropy on ARM": the Trusted Firmware-A EL3-to-EL2 trap forwarder, the Linux/KVM per-process dispatch patches, the guest monitor module, the rr.soft RNDR/RNDRRS substitution engine, test harnesses, the substrate-survey probe, and the raw demonstration evidence captured on the stock QEMU v11.1.0 release. title: Heesch numbers and maximal coronas of small polyforms with certificates and a Lean-verified SAT encoding
abstract: Article (version 2.1) with records, code and a Lean formalization. For a fixed selection of 3,964 shapes from Kaplan's tables of unmarked polyominoes, polyhexes and polyiamonds, every Heesch number Hc and Hh is given a corona witness (checked by two geometric checkers) and an upper-bound CNF whose unsatisfiability proof is accepted by drat-trim (5,019 proofs). A Lean 4 theorem proves the SAT encoding sound on the square, hexagonal and triangular grids (six statements, standard axioms, six kernel runs with five implementations), and a recorded finite comparison connects all 5,019 checked CNF files to the Lean definition; a second encoding agrees on every value. Maximal coronas of 22 shapes are counted by two implementations (complete agreement in 28 of 30 combinations), and a restricted search of 3,442 polyominoes with 20-28 cells yields no finite Hh=4 example. drat-trim and the file comparison are outside Lean; no human expert review. Text and data: CC BY 4.0; code: Apache 2.0.

title: Explanation Multiplicity in SHAP: Characterization and Assessment — Data and Experimental Results
abstract: This record contains the saved experimental outputs and supporting data for “Explanation Multiplicity in SHAP: Characterization and Assessment,” accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Evaluations and Datasets Track. The study examines variation in SHAP explanations across model and explainer realizations, using magnitude-based, rank-based, and set-based metrics calibrated against randomized reference models. This archive provides stored explanations, prediction probabilities, dataset inputs, and supporting model checkpoints for the analyses reported in the paper. The archive contains seven top-level directories: results_tree/: Saved explanation outputs used in the main analyses and the Arrhythmia experiment. results_true/: Full-training-background reference explanations used in the reference comparisons. background_results/: Saved outputs from the background-size experiments. results_conditional/: Conditional and marginal explanation outputs for the appendix comparison. proba/: Saved prediction-probability files. dataset/: Dataset input and target files used by the experiments and analyses. models_cpu/: CPU-trained model checkpoints used in the conditional and marginal comparison. To use these files, extract the archive into the root of the accompanying code repository. Preserve the directory structure, including the nested proba/proba/ directory. Analysis notebooks, environment information, and instructions are provided in the repository. Some directories preserve alternative saved outputs. Use the repository’s documented loaders and input-selection rules to reproduce the paper’s analyses; not every archived file is used in every figure. The reported background-size sweep extends to K = 1600, subject to the available training-set size. This deposit preserves the existing OSF archive without regenerating explanations or predictions. The original OSF copy remains available. Code and analysis notebooks Paper Original OSF archive Third-party datasets remain subject to the terms of their original sources.

title: Dual context attentive feature network: an interpretable dual-pathway deep learning framework for accurate gastrointestinal endoscopic image classification
abstract: Background: Gastrointestinal (GI) diseases such as colorectal cancer and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) contribute substantially to global morbidity, with colorectal cancer accounting for nearly 10% of all cancer diagnoses worldwide. Many existing artificial intelligence (AI) models suffer from limited generalizability and poor clinical interpretability. This study aimed to develop and evaluate an explainable AI (XAI) framework for classifying GI diseases from endoscopic images. Methods: Public datasets from the Simula Research Laboratory were used: Hyper-Kvasir (10,662 images) for training, Kvasir-V1 (4,000 images) for validation, and Kvasir-V2 (8,000 images) as an independent test set. Two convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures, GastroNet-dilated multi-scale attention (DMSA) (a proposed DMSA Network) and M2ShallowNet (a lightweight hybrid model), were designed for complementary feature extraction. Deep features were fused using a dual context attentive feature network (DCAF-Net) followed by Aquila Optimizer (AO)-based feature-weight refinement without introducing additional trainable fusion parameters. Performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, and statistical testing. Interpretability was examined using gradient-weighted class activation mapping++ (Grad-CAM++) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Results: The best-performing classifier, a multilayer perceptron (MLP), achieved an accuracy of 97.21%, precision of 97.27%, recall of 97.21%, Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 96.82%, and F1-score of 97.21% on the independent test set. ROC analysis demonstrated excellent class separability, and statistical testing confirmed reliable generalization. XAI results highlighted regions that qualitatively correspond to pathological areas; formal clinical validation of these interpretations was not performed in this study. Conclusions: The proposed framework offers a promising research prototype for AI-assisted GI disease classification. Its potential for real-world endoscopic deployment requires further prospective validation before clinical adoption.

title: SecondThought: Confidence-Gated Reasoning for Tool Calls in Small Local Models
abstract: Reads a tool call's own token log-probabilities to decide when a small model should think before calling a tool. Thinking on the least confident 30% of requests keeps most of the gain of always thinking at about half the output tokens, and avoids thinking's tendency to call tools when none fit. Includes code, all responses on BFCL with Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B, and the paper.

title: Detectores pasivos de texto generado: la cifra de la ficha no es la del caso / Passive detectors of generated text: the datasheet figure is not the case figure
abstract: Los detectores pasivos de texto generado se presentan con una cifra: un AUROC, una exactitud o una tasa de falsos positivos. Este artículo pregunta qué conserva esa cifra cuando el texto que se juzga no pertenece al banco donde se midió. Se sintetizan siete estudios técnicos y seis documentos de proveedores e instituciones, cotejados en sus versiones primarias el 29 de septiembre de 2026. Dentro de su banco, los detectores de referencia alcanzan valores altos. Fuera de él, la evidencia muestra tres cosas distintas: la exactitud a un falso positivo fijado cae de forma drástica en algunas combinaciones de generador y decodificación; un detector con buena discriminación puede, con su umbral por defecto, clasificar como máquina a la mayoría de los textos humanos de un dominio nuevo; y el falso positivo medido en 2023 sobre ensayos de estudiantes de inglés como segunda lengua fue muy superior al de los nativos. Esa última diferencia no es una ley: una replicación de 2026 con un producto encuentra una brecha menor en inglés y ninguna diferencia significativa en checo, y otro detector no separa ensayos de segunda lengua corregidos y sin corregir. Las fichas de proveedores consultadas no declaran el cruce de dominio, y dos universidades españolas, una universidad estadounidense y un caso de COPE niegan valor probatorio o de umbral a la puntuación. Se propone distinguir precisión de ficha y error del caso, y uso de triaje y uso de prueba. No se aportan experimentos nuevos ni instrucciones para evadir detectores. English abstract: Passive detectors of machine-generated text are usually summarised by a single figure: an AUROC, an accuracy or a false-positive rate. This paper asks what that figure retains when the text being judged does not belong to the benchmark on which it was measured. It synthesises seven technical studies and six vendor and institutional documents, checked against their primary versions on 29 September 2026. Within their own benchmarks, reference detectors reach high values. Outside them, the evidence shows three different things: accuracy at a fixed false-positive rate falls drastically for some combinations of generator and decoding; a detector with good discrimination can, at its default threshold, classify most human texts from a new domain as machine-written; and the false-positive rate measured in 2023 on essays by students of English as a second language was far higher than for native writers. The last gap is not a law: a 2026 replication with one product finds a smaller gap in English and no significant difference in Czech, and another detector does not separate corrected from uncorrected second-language essays. The vendor datasheets consulted do not state cross-domain performance, and two Spanish universities, a US university and a COPE case deny the score any evidentiary or threshold value. The paper proposes distinguishing datasheet accuracy from case error, and triage use from evidence use. No new experiments and no instructions for evading detectors are provided. Working paper de la serie WHITE-PAPERS (wp-2026-041, v0.9). Incluye versión en español e inglés. No revisado por pares. Uso de herramientas de IA declarado en el manuscrito; sin conflictos de interés ni financiación.

title: HYBRID PHOTONIC COMPUTING FOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE From Nanophotonics Physics to System Level Integration
abstract: This document presents a rigorous, physics-grounded framework for Hybrid Photonic Computing in AI, shifting the narrative from academic illusions to realistic engineering. It debunks myths of infinite energy savings, proving that after accounting for converters, lasers, and cooling, realistic efficiency gains are 5x to 10x, with a 200x latency improvement for linear operations. Grounded in Maxwell’s equations, it addresses constraints like Two-Photon Absorption and thermal crosstalk. The solution is a hybrid architecture: photonics handles linear matrix multiplications, while electronics manage non-linear activations. Innovations like Phase Change Materials enable zero-static-power in-memory computing, breaking the Von Neumann bottleneck. Crucially, the work advocates for hardware-software co-design, introducing photonics-aware training algorithms that inject hardware noise to build resilience. Finally, it identifies photonic packaging as the true industrial bottleneck, offering a pragmatic roadmap toward commercially viable, heterogeneous, and physics-aware computing systems.

title: Teleporting Energy via Quantum Entanglement on Superconducting Hardware — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: FINDING: Quantum teleportation transfers quantum *states* (information) via entanglement, not matter/energy; recent work extends this to teleporting *physical quantities* (energy) on superconducting hardware. | MATH: Core protocol uses Bell-state measurement (maximally entangled basis, dimension d=2 for qubits; generalized to d-dimensions), classical communication of 2 bits per teleported qubit, and unitary correction U ∈ {I, X, Z, XZ}. Fidelity F = |⟨ψ|ρ_out|ψ⟩|² ≥ 2/3 for classical bound; experimental fidelities often >0.9. Energy teleportation (arXiv:2301.02666) uses a quantum energy teleportation (QET) protocol: local measurement on one qubit of an entangled pair, then conditional unitary on the other, extracting positive energy ΔE > 0 from the vacuum/ground state. Key quantity: conditional mutual information or entanglement entropy S(ρ_A) − S(ρ_AB) governs extractable energy. | CONNECTION: Bell states are eigenvectors of Pauli matrices — roots of SU(2), isomorphic to quaternions ( Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: A Starting Score Is Not a Ceiling: When Accuracy Before Reinforcement Learning Predicts Accuracy After It, Why Each Proposed Replacement Sees a Different Failure, and the Axis Test That Decides Which Proxy to Trust
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research Reasoning models are usually built in two stages, supervised fine-tuning and then reinforcement learning against a verifier, and the first stage is usually judged by the benchmark accuracy of its checkpoint. An August 2026 study reports that the strategy with by far the lowest accuracy before reinforcement learning finished with the highest accuracy after it, and concludes that pre-RL accuracy is not a reliable indicator of post-RL potential. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the conclusion is right about the instrument and too broad about its failure. Arithmetic on that study's own tables shows that the whole reversal comes from one candidate whose output format had been disrupted: the four format-stable strategies keep the same order before and after reinforcement learning on the nine-benchmark mean, and pass@32, the replacement proxy proposed elsewhere, ranks the disrupted candidate last as well. Across the wider record, starting accuracy ranks candidates correctly when they differ in how much fresh data they saw, and fails when they differ in repetition, homogeneity, behavioural repertoire or output format, axes along which pass@1 and reinforcement-learning readiness come apart. Each proposed replacement, pass@k at large k, held-out validation loss, behaviour and faithfulness probes, early curve fits, sees one of these failure channels and is blind to at least one other, and "post-RL accuracy" is itself indexed by the reinforcement-learning budget and readout. The paper consolidates 22 published results in a table and a figure, states an axis-first decision procedure for choosing a proxy, and specifies five studies that would settle what remains open.

title: Big J's original quantum circuit (TEQA v3.2) on a real IBM quantum computer (23 October 2026)
abstract: Big J's original quantum circuit layer (TEQA v3.2; teqa_circuit_v32.py, SHA-256 4907aa40...8218) run on a real IBM quantum computer, ibm_fez, on 23 October 2026, to see whether the chip gives Big J the same call as the simulator. Per neuron a 25-qubit genome circuit runs first and its measured counts feed an 8-qubit neural circuit; seven neurons vote. Rules were written and fingerprinted before each run. Run 1, the three locked inputs: same call on 3 of 3, neuron votes 20 of 21 (PASS). Run 2, twenty new inputs: same call on 17 of 20 against a pass mark of 16, every strong call 15 of 15, neuron votes 114 of 140 (PASS). The three misses were borderline inputs that came out negative on the chip. Sampler, no error mitigation; 59 quantum seconds in total on IBM's Open Plan. The record holds the circuit file, plans, locks, run scripts, IBM job IDs, per-neuron results and SHA-256 fingerprints of every file. Patent pending: US provisional application 64/179,295, filed 19 October 2026. Further rights reserved.

title: Derechos de autor y entrenamiento de modelos: actos separables y reserva sin comprobación / Copyright and model training: separable acts and a reservation without verification
abstract: El debate sobre derechos de autor y entrenamiento de modelos suele resumirse en dos titulares opuestos: que entrenar ya es lícito o que ya está prohibido. Este artículo lee en su texto oficial las resoluciones y normas que más se citan sobre texto e imagen y pregunta qué acto califica cada una. Se distinguen cuatro actos: el acceso a la copia, su uso para entrenar, la retención de la obra en los pesos o en la salida y la sustitución de la obra en su mercado. En Estados Unidos, tres autos de distrito califican esos actos por separado y con resultados distintos: el uso de notas editoriales para un competidor no generativo no fue fair use, y el Tercer Circuito lo confirmó con una opinión que distingue expresamente los modelos generativos; el entrenamiento de un modelo generativo con libros sí lo fue en dos casos, aunque no la conservación de copias pirata, y uno de ellos limita su alcance a trece autores. Un acuerdo de clase posterior transige insumos pasados sin liberar salidas. En el Reino Unido, la sentencia Getty declara que los pesos no son una copia infractora y no juzga el entrenamiento. En la Unión Europea, la excepción de minería se aplica salvo reserva del titular, y el Reglamento de IA exige una política y un resumen, pero descarta un examen obra por obra. La contraevidencia principal es un auto que, en términos generales, anticipa que copiar para entrenar será ilegal en la mayoría de los casos. La contribución es una matriz de actos y un inventario de entrenamiento por acto, ambos de elaboración propia y sin validación. No se analizan recursos pendientes, contratos no publicados ni la comprobación técnica de si una obra está en los pesos. English abstract: Debates on copyright and model training are often reduced to two opposite headlines: that training is already lawful, or that it is already prohibited. This paper reads the most cited decisions and rules on text and images in their official text and asks which act each of them addresses. Four acts are distinguished: access to the copy, its use for training, retention of the work in the weights or the output, and substitution for the work in its market. In the United States, three district court orders assess these acts separately and reach different results: using editorial headnotes for a non-generative competitor was not fair use, and the Third Circuit affirmed in an opinion that expressly distinguishes generative models; training a generative model on books was fair use in two cases, although keeping pirated copies was not, and one of those orders limits its reach to thirteen authors. A later class settlement releases past inputs without releasing outputs. In the United Kingdom, Getty holds that the model weights are not an infringing copy and does not decide training. In the European Union, the text and data mining exception applies unless the rightholder has reserved the use, and the AI Act requires a policy and a summary while ruling out a work-by-work assessment. The main counter-evidence is an order that, in general terms, expects copying for training to be unlawful in most cases. The contribution is an act matrix and an act-based training inventory, both the author's own proposals without validation. Pending appeals, unpublished contracts and the technical question of whether a work is present in the weights are outside the scope. Working paper de la serie WHITE-PAPERS (wp-2026-030, v0.9). Incluye versión en español e inglés. No revisado por pares. Uso de herramientas de IA declarado en el manuscrito; sin conflictos de interés ni financiación.

title: A Unified Framework for Image-to-3D Part Generation via Variable Granularity
abstract: Controllable 3D part generation is pivotal for digital asset creation, yet existing methods lack the flexibility to accommodate diverse user workflows requiring varying levels of control. In this paper, we introduce FlexPart, a unified image-to-3D part generation framework that supports variable-granularity geometric conditions within a single model. By seamlessly integrating heterogeneous inputs, ranging from sparse points to dense bounding boxes and masks, via gated adaptive modulation, FlexPart unlocks a powerful cross-modal synergy. We also propose an asymmetric geometric guidance mechanism that leverages strong spatial priors to align representations across granularities, improving geometric consistency and facilitating inter-task synergy. Under mask conditioning on PartVerseXL, FlexPart reduces Part CD by 16.6% relative to TripoSG + SAM3D and by 10.5% relative to OmniPart, while maintaining competitive whole-mesh quality. The code can be found at https://github.com/Gucci233/FlexPart

title: Reading, Writing, Sharing, and Interacting with the World through Video
abstract: Video foundation models have advanced rapidly in understanding and generating visual sequences, while video world models seek to capture the underlying dynamics of the world they depict. Despite their different objectives, both concern the relationship between video observations and an evolving world. This survey adopts world modeling as a unifying lens for examining these developments. Viewing an observed video as a partial, lossy, and temporally ordered projection of a latent temporal world, we organize the literature around four complementary operations: reading infers world properties from observed video; writing synthesizes video from specified or learned world conditions; sharing integrates understanding and generation through common modeling mechanisms; and interacting predicts and updates world states under actions and evolving observations. This perspective distinguishes temporal coherence in observed or generated sequences from consistency in the underlying world state. Across tasks, representations, models, datasets, and benchmarks, we trace a shift in emphasis from clip-level recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and evaluation grounded in interaction and downstream decisions, and we distill the open challenges that follow.

title: BrickWright: Agentic Creation of Physically Feasible Brick Builds
abstract: Frontier coding agents are becoming increasingly adept at 3D modeling. Yet, they still face challenges when building objects meant to be assembled in the physical world, often creating invalid assemblies with floating, colliding, or disconnected parts. We argue that providing agents with tools for assembling builds and verifying their physical feasibility is sufficient for them to produce physically valid assemblies that still adhere to input prompts. Focusing on the domain of LEGO brick builds, we present BrickWright, a framework for generating physically feasible brick builds from text or image prompts using pre-trained agents, where a build is physically feasible if it uses only real parts, has no colliding or floating parts, and forms a connected structure if possible. BrickWright guides agents to create builds by writing code with BrickLayer, a Python toolkit with two main components: an ergonomic brick assembly API that halves inference cost compared to working in raw LDraw, and a validator that provides feedback on physical feasibility. Whereas baseline agents achieve physical validity rates ranging from only 9% (GPT-6 Luna) to 69% (GPT-6 Astra), BrickWright-guided agents achieve 100% validity on a sample of 512 prompts, while improving prompt adherence for lightweight agents and maintaining it for stronger agents. Additionally, they outperform specialized models on the text-to-brick task. Code is available on our project page: https://avalovelace1.github.io/brickwright/

title: Different Tasks, Different Timesteps: Temporal Task-Aware Quantization for Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) introduce unique quantization challenges due to their iterative denoising process. In this work, we reveal that quantization sensitivity is both taskand time-dependent, with different downstream tasks exhibiting distinct precision requirements across denoising steps. We further show that these patterns can be predicted without groundtruth labels or task-specific evaluation metrics. Building on these findings, we introduce T 2Quant, a task and time-aware mixedprecision quantization framework that uses a label-free sensitivity signal to optimally allocate activation precision across denoising steps under a fixed bit-width budget. Extensive experiments across three DLMs and six benchmarks demonstrate that T 2Quant consistently improves the average accuracy of existing quantization methods, achieving gains of up to 6.7 percentage points under the same budget.

title: A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy
abstract: Standard implementations of softmax, log-softmax, and cross-entropy have two numerical bugs. The first bug, Softmax Collapse, rounds the target logit's gradient to zero if that one logit is much larger than the others, resulting in gradients that no longer sum to zero. The second bug, Softmax Cancellation, occurs when student logits are close to teacher logits, and produces non-zero gradients even when the student and teacher logits are equal. We present simple implementations of log-softmax, softmax, and cross-entropy that fix both bugs. Our fix eliminates the previously-observed "Slingshot" phenomenon, speeds up grokking with weight decay, prevents accuracy collapse without weight decay, stops student networks from drifting away from the teacher during distillation, and shows that after memorization, logit growth is bounded by an equilibrium between weight decay and Adam's $ε$ hyperparameter.

title: UniVOE: A Removal-Driven Framework for Interaction-Aware Universal Video Object Editing
abstract: Video object removal and injection are reciprocal editing operations between object-present and object-absent video states, yet they differ substantially in training difficulty. Removal can be effectively bootstrapped from video inpainting and further adapted to erase object-related interaction effects. Injection, however, requires large-scale paired supervision to model object appearance, dynamics, and scene-dependent effects, while perfectly aligned real-world pairs are difficult to collect and synthetic data lacks sufficient realism and diversity. To address this challenge, we present UniVOE, a removal-driven framework for training both video object removal and injection models. We first train an effect-aware remover by transferring video inpainting priors and finetuning on object-present/object-absent pairs. The trained remover converts real object-present videos into object-absent counterparts, creating large-scale paired supervision for injection. An injection model is trained on these pairs in the reverse direction to recover objects together with their dynamics and interaction effects. Moreover, since pixel-level reconstruction alone cannot adequately capture perceptual realism, we introduce a reward-based post-training method that aligns injection results with human preferences using a proprietary reward model. Experiments against strong open-source and commercial systems demonstrate that UniVOE achieves state-of-the-art performance on both object removal and injection, particularly in challenging interaction-effect cases.

title: Memory before Goal: Role of Pre-History Memory for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation in dynamic scenes is non-Markovian: cues vanish as objects change or are hidden, or leave the view as the robot turns and walks, yet whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies see only the present. We present WholeBodyMem, an object-guided perceptual memory that keeps the pre-history of object events seen before the robot acts on its goal. SAM3 tracks the task objects, and their events causally select key frames within an adaptive budget, which the action expert reads by cross-attention together with object tokens encoding appearance, geometry and time. We also contribute HuMeGo, a humanoid memory benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks. Keeping the right frames rather than more frames, WholeBodyMem surpasses memoryless and uniform-memory baselines, raising its base policy's success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and from 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot, while also improving the standard SIMPLE tasks (70.2% to 86.9%).

title: Rethinking Sequence Compression with Test-time Regression
abstract: Sequence compression is a fundamental operation and a critical information bottleneck in efficient language and multimodal models, and yet prevailing approaches based on pooling or learned projections remain underperforming. We revisit sequence compression through the lens of test-time regression: input tokens define a regression problem whose fitted coefficients form the compressed representation. Importantly, the regression problem is learned end-to-end via backpropagation, while its coefficients are computed efficiently in closed form during the forward pass. This leads to TTR-Compressor, a general alternative to conventional pooling and projection-based compression. We evaluate TTR-Compressor as the compressor for block-wise sparse attention and the visual token merger for multimodal large language models. On block-wise sparse attention, TTR-Compressor improves RULER performance over attention-based compressors by a large margin. For visual token merging, it consistently outperforms the standard MLP merger and matches its performance with 55.6% fewer visual tokens. These results establish test-time regression as an effective primitive for sequence compression in efficient language and multimodal models.

evidence.abstract: Sequence compression is a fundamental operation and a critical information bottleneck in efficient language and multimodal models, and yet prevailing approaches based on pooling or learned projections remain underperforming. We revisit sequence compression through the lens of test-time regression: input tokens define a regression problem whose fitted coefficients form the compressed representation. Importantly, the regression problem is learned end-to-end via backpropagation, while its coefficients are computed efficiently in closed form during the forward pass. This leads to TTR-Compressor, a general alternative to conventional pooling and projection-based compression. We evaluate TTR-Compressor as the compressor for block-wise sparse attention and the visual token merger for multimodal large language models. On block-wise sparse attention, TTR-Compressor improves RULER performance over attention-based compressors by a large margin. For visual token merging, it consistently outperforms the standard MLP merger and matches its performance with 55.6% fewer visual tokens. These results establish test-time regression as an effective primitive for sequence compression in efficient language and multimodal models.

title: F2G-Pose: Geometry-Aware Foundation Feature Lifting for Direct RGB-D Category-Level Object Pose Estimation
abstract: This paper studies category-level RGB-D object pose estimation, which recovers an object's 3D rotation and translation without instance-specific CAD models or reference views. This task is highly ambiguous due to intra-class variations, symmetries, and partial observations. Current solutions struggle to balance reliability and efficiency: methods based on intermediate structures are prone to error propagation, while diffusion models suffer from high inference latency and complex post-hoc candidate extraction. To address this, we present F2G-Pose, a real-time direct, single-pass framework that predicts category-level pose, metric size, and camera-frame completed shape from a single RGB-D observation in one feed-forward pass. F2G-Pose lifts dense visual foundation features to partial point clouds, encodes local geometry with DGCNN tokenization, and integrates object-level structure with a Mixture-of-Experts Transformer. Joint size prediction and camera-frame shape completion encourage metric consistency through dense geometric supervision. With its task-specific network trained only on pose-annotated synthetic SOPE data and its frozen RADIO backbone externally pretrained, F2G-Pose achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on SOPE and ROPE while running at 28 FPS for pose-only inference, and further demonstrates strong camera-frame geometry on HouseCat6D and real-object transfer on HANDAL. Analyses of latency, robustness, shape completion, and GenPose++ candidate behavior further demonstrate the efficiency and reliability of F2G-Pose, with real-world manipulation experiments demonstrating deployment potential under segmented RGB-D inputs. The project page, code, and pretrained models are made available at https://jrryzh.github.io/F2G-Pose/.

title: OP-Print: Tracing Membership Imprints in On-Policy Self-Distillation
abstract: On-policy distillation has been widely adopted for alleviating the distribution mismatch of off-policy distillation. Self-distillation further removes the need for an external teacher by using the student's own outputs, enhanced with extra context or demonstrations, as supervision. This teacher-free design makes on-policy self-distillation practical, yet its privacy risks remain largely unexplored. In particular, using two coupled views of the same training example may strengthen its memorization. Motivated by this, we present the first study of membership inference attacks against on-policy self-distillation. We investigate both gray-box and black-box threat models and propose a unified attack framework, named OP-Print. OP-Print builds on our finding that the supervision imprint in on-policy self-distillation is sparse and structured, concentrating on uncertainty-sensitive correction sites rather than across the entire rollout. Exploiting this property, we construct attack signals tailored to the two access levels: in the gray-box setting, OP-Print directly aggregates the privileged teacher-student residual correction along the same rollout; in the black-box setting, it measures restart-based output-basin stability as an observable surrogate for the hidden correction process. Across diverse models and distillation schemes, all baseline attacks remain essentially at random guessing even under gray-box access, whereas OP-Print is broadly validated to be effective in both gray-box and black-box settings.

title: Beyond Watching and Searching: Benchmarking Agents for Video-centered Deep Research Reports
abstract: Deep research agents synthesize open-web evidence into long reports, but current benchmarks do not evaluate research centered on a source video. We introduce Video-Centered Deep Research Report Generation. Given a video and user request, an agent identifies research questions, retrieves external multimodal evidence, and produces an interactive report linked to relevant video moments. This task has direct practical value because it helps users locate relevant moments, verify claims, reproduce demonstrated procedures, and make informed decisions from video content. We present a skill-based workflow and OmniDR-Bench for this task. For evaluation, we propose Omni Atomic Rubric Trees (Omni-ARTs). Each tree contains three dimensions, 23 shared directions, and task-specific atomic binary criteria. The directions test audiovisual grounding, multimodal evidence use, and interactive presentation. Audited Rubric Construction (ARC) builds these trees through independent evidence collection, automated checks, behavioral calibration, and iterative human review. OmniDR-Bench contains 50 Chinese and English tasks across 19 realworld subcategories. It includes 6,414 criteria. Across 18 agent configurations, the best system scores 63.3 out of 100. Current agents still need broader content coverage, stronger causal and logical analysis across modalities, and more accurate citation support. We further analyze models, harnesses, skill configurations, video categories, and research trajectories. The code and data are released at https://github.com/marinero4972/OmniDR-Bench.

title: What Makes a Good Unmasking Policy? A Controlled Study of Learned Unmasking in Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Masked diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, but their efficiency depends on which predictions are committed. Learned unmasking policies improve the speed--accuracy trade-off, yet differ in supervision, inputs, and capacity, obscuring which choices matter. We view supervised policies as distilling a decoding procedure through a teacher and examine independently what the teacher labels as committable, on which states the policy imitates it, what the policy observes, and how much the number of function evaluations (NFE) must decrease to offset policy overhead. We find that labeling predictions matching the final output is overly permissive at low NFE, and hidden states are weak alone but can complement confidence. About a 10% NFE reduction suffices to offset policy overhead for policies up to 7.5M parameters across tested settings. We therefore train a policy on trajectory-contraction targets, which accept only commitments staying on a reference trajectory, using confidence and hidden states. On LLaDA-8B-Instruct, the resulting 856K-parameter policy achieves the best accuracy--NFE frontier and highest throughput on GSM8K, is competitive at moderate targets on MATH-500 and HumanEval, and largely transfers to Dream-7B-Instruct.

title: Social-HUMINT: An LLM-Augmented Unified Framework for Measuring Social Media Exposure
abstract: In the post-API landscape, social-media profiling has become inexpensive and automated: Large Language Models (LLMs) can extract structured information from unstructured content and deduce attributes users never disclosed. A person's true exposure is not what they post but what can be inferred from it. As these practices become routine, exposure to social engineering attacks becomes an operational certainty, demanding a shared framework for assessment and mitigation. We make this exposure measurable by quantifying how accurately a target can be profiled, and how far that profile enables social engineering attacks. Because no existing model fully spans this continuum, we unify Social Media Intelligence (SOCMINT) and Cyber Human Intelligence (Cyber-HUMINT), two individual-focused disciplines that evolved separately, into a single doctrine-grounded taxonomy of 38 capabilities across the Cyber Threat Intelligence lifecycle, where user profiling bridges passive collection and active engagement. Domain experts validated the taxonomy (Fleiss' $κ$ = 0.92). We operationalize its core path (extraction, inference, and susceptibility assessment) as an LLM-augmented multi-agent pipeline, evaluated on real participants' public data. Susceptibility is assessed indirectly: the pipeline predicts how each target would rank personalized engagement options, matching their actual choices significantly above chance. This ranking capacity captures the personalization on which tailored attacks depend. The underlying profiles are accurate: extraction reaches F1 = 97.3%, and inferred attributes score 4.73/5, both far above rule-based and NER-based baselines at negligible cost. The framework augments security analysts' tradecraft rather than replacing it and enables defenders to gauge their own exposure before an adversary does.

title: AgentVQA: A Unified Benchmark for Agentic Visual Understanding
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can perform a broad range of tasks across diverse settings, yet their performance in agentic contexts remains poorly understood. Although online evaluations in simulators and real-world environments are essential for measuring interactive agent performance, they are costly and challenging to scale. Complementary offline VQA benchmarks can enable faster and more reliable comparisons across agentic domains, yet existing benchmarks remain limited and fragmented. To address this gap, we introduce AgentVQA, an offline benchmark for evaluating VLMs on realistic agentic scenarios across five agent domains: Web Agents, Robotics, Egocentric Videos, Games, and Spatial Planning. We build AgentVQA by manually selecting 1000 challenging, real-world agent examples from 23 source datasets and adapting them for reliable offline evaluation. The resulting benchmark preserves realistic scenarios from interactive environments across diverse domains, and its model rankings track those from corresponding online evaluations. Across the 22 evaluated models, the best achieves only 58.5% accuracy. Our cross-domain analysis shows that errors are driven primarily by failures to ground and maintain accurate representations of the current and evolving visual state, including localizing relevant UI elements, interpreting motion, tracking state changes over time, and inferring 3D spatial relationships, rather than by task misinterpretation or downstream logical reasoning.

title: AnyGameRenderer: Entity-Consistent Generative Rendering Across Games and an Entity-Level Benchmark
abstract: AI coding agents can now build small playable games in minutes, but the results usually look like programmer art: gray blockouts, colored geometric primitives, and flat semantic blobs. We present AnyGameRenderer, a video-to-video generative renderer that turns such footage into high-quality visuals with characters, motion detail, and effects. Throughout, it keeps the layout, camera, and every entity's position and timing intact. Our AnyGameRenderer generalizes across a wide range of genres that agents build, such as tower defense, auto-battlers, top-down survivors, turn-based battles, kart racing, and crowd runners. AnyGameRenderer takes plain video as its game-state input, with no complex representations such as engine G-buffers, per-object class labels, or low-poly proxies. Gray blockouts, colored primitives, semantic maps, and wireframes all work as input. It also preserves entity correspondence: group counts stay correct, and entities appear and disappear on the right frame. We implement AnyGameRenderer by LoRA fine-tuning MiniMax-H3 ref2va, a 33B reference-video-conditioned video generation model. Training uses $\sim$10k paired clips from three sources: (i) multi-stream rendering data from 38 agent-made games exported from GEAR, an AI game-creation tool; (ii) two-stream rendering data from Unreal Engine, with programmatically controlled crowds, count changes, and entity scales; and (iii) real gameplay recordings, with pairs reconstructed via 3D-box detection. To evaluate the entity correspondence, we propose an entity-level benchmark of 59 held-out cases with 753 entities, scored against ground-truth boxes. Compared with the base model, AnyGameRenderer better preserves entity correspondence: temporal match rises from 50.9\% to 62.9\%, missed count changes fall from 34.7\% to 21.3\%, and fewer entities are hallucinated or left unrendered.

title: SCOPE: Compiling Natural-Language Policies into Neurosymbolic Predicate Programs
abstract: Policy enforcement for LLM agents has shifted from single-turn content moderation to compound, application-specific policies evaluated over multi-turn transcripts and tool-call trajectories. Fine-tuned guardrail models are efficient but degrade on compound policies, and while LLM-as-a-judge approaches achieve higher accuracy, they incur high inference cost and tend to produce unstable predictions. Neurosymbolic methods offer a natural alternative, decomposing the policy into narrow neural decisions composed under explicit logic. However, existing symbolic layers lack the required expressiveness and are optimized against fixed data rather than the policy itself. To address this, we introduce SCOPE, which compiles a policy into an executable program of neural predicates executed by small models, deterministic extractors, and code that composes their outputs. We evaluate SCOPE on a benchmark of real-world policy tasks against prompt optimization, task decomposition, and workflow generation methods, achieving the highest average accuracy across tasks and models. Programs optimized with the weakest executor transfer to other models without further optimization. This allows them to be deployed in production on inexpensive models, where they reach accuracy comparable to frontier reasoning models. Unlike these monolithic models, SCOPE produces substantially more stable predictions, and each verdict is interpretable through the predicate outputs that produced it. title: FocusVLA: Future-Intent Guided Dynamic View Routing for Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have become an important paradigm for robotic manipulation by unifying visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. Since reliable manipulation requires sufficient observation of objects, end-effectors, and their spatial relationships, multi-view inputs are widely used to provide complementary spatial information. However, our experiments show that existing VLA models do not fully exploit such multi-view complementarity. The policy tends to persistently rely on the wrist view, lacking the ability to dynamically adjust global-local view dependency across manipulation stages, which limits stage adaptability and robustness. To address this issue, we propose FocusVLA, a stage-aware multi-view routing framework. FocusVLA predicts future interaction intent from historical actions and uses it to guide dynamic view routing during action generation. By adaptively coordinating global and local observations across different task stages, FocusVLA improves multi-view utilization. On RoboTwin 2.0, FocusVLA improves the average success rate over the strongest baseline $π_{0.5}$ by 10.10 pp. In real-world evaluation, FocusVLA improves the success rate from 71.7\% to 85.0\%, achieving a 13.3\% gain over $π_{0.5}$. Moreover, the intent prediction and dynamic routing modules of FocusVLA can be integrated into existing VLA frameworks without modifying their core architectures.

title: Padding to k: A Minimum Count in the Schema Makes Open-Weight Models Pad Their Extraction Lists
abstract: Extraction pipelines ask language models for JSON that follows a schema, and the schema can set a minimum number of list entries. We ask what models do when the document holds fewer items than that minimum. Under a preregistered plan, we test eight open-weight models on 558 real documents from nine annotated datasets, with six more models on hosted services as a reference. Three findings stand out. First, models treat the count as a target: a minimum shown in the schema, but not enforced, raises the share of lists longer than the true count from 34.5% to 55.4%. Second, the padding is hard to catch, because most added entries are real text taken from the document; about half of them pass a check that each entry occurs in the source. Third, common fixes help only partly: a line saying fewer items are fine removes the effect on average but misses more true items, a count in prose ("up to k") also raises over-counting, an "N/A" option under an enforced minimum still leaves half the lists padded, and re-asking with the validation error makes padding far more common. We release the code, answer lists and run records at https://github.com/AbhishekBarali/padding-to-k

title: Joint or Per-Option? Compact Encoders for Closed-Set Decisions from 17 Million to 1 Billion Parameters
abstract: Many language-model pipelines end in a closed-set decision, such as selecting a tool. Prompting a large language model for it is slow and order-sensitive. We ask how small an encoder for such decisions can be and whether it should read the options jointly or separately. In a three-seed study at 32 million parameters, per-option scoring beats joint scoring on a held-out sample of a 37-benchmark decision suite by 5.8 points of chance-corrected skill at matched optimizer steps and by 2.8 at approximately matched training compute; two external benchmarks agree, though not significantly on their unseen tasks. Crossing reader with initialisation shows that the advantage requires a reranker initialisation, whose query-candidate pair input matches per-option reading; from the raw encoder the two readers are indistinguishable. Per-option scoring needs 5 to 13 times more encoder passes: at most twice the median latency, but more than four times the mean. Of six released joint encoders (17 million to 1 billion parameters), the 68- and 150-million-parameter models exceed a 435-million-parameter DeBERTa-v3 zero-shot classifier by 4.9 and 5.9 accuracy points on 209 overlap-audited System1-Arena tasks and are at least on par with it on the 145 tasks unseen in training. The smallest answers a median request in 14 milliseconds on 16 processor threads, against 728 for the classifier. Reordering options changes 12 to 23% of the joint models' answers (per-option scoring: none). Up to 68 million parameters, they lead their size range on a public leaderboard's private, mainly in-distribution tests.

title: IQuest-Q1: Advancing Foundation Capabilities for Agentic CLI Systems
abstract: We present IQuest-Q1, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) agentic foundation model with 320B total parameters (15B activated). IQuest-Q1 is developed through a three-stage process: (1) stable and efficient pre-training, combining Stable SplitNorm, Muon, and muP with a two-stage curriculum whose second stage increases the coding-data mixture, preserving a wide stability margin between safe and optimal learning rates; (2) fine-grained mid-training, expanding the data mixture across domains and formats and progressively extending the context; and (3) multi-scaffold with multi-version post-training, combining SFT, domain-specialized RL, and MOPD across various scaffolds to integrate complementary training signals and strengthen agentic coding capabilities. Furthermore, model merging combines different experts and checkpoints from different stages while mitigating conflicts among their parameter updates. The resulting IQuest-Q1 demonstrates capabilities in both coding and general tasks. We release IQuest-Q1 as an open-source model to support community research and development.

title: GateFormer: Forecast-Space Decomposition for Intra-Hour Solar Irradiance Prediction from Sky Images
abstract: Sub-hourly dispatch, balancing, and storage control increasingly depend on forecasts that anticipate rapid variability in solar generation. Accurate sky-image-based irradiance forecasting requires a combination of visual cloud dynamics with recent irradiance state while adapting to different short-term irradiance-change regimes. To address this, we introduce GateFormer, a GHI-conditioned dual-decoder ViT for intra-hour global horizontal irradiance (GHI) forecasting through forecast-space decomposition. GateFormer embeds observed GHI into the visual token stream, allowing interaction with sky-image patch features through self-attention. From this shared representation, a Trajectory Head predicts future GHI sequence, while a Delta Head predicts final-horizon change from the latest observed GHI. The two final-horizon forecasts are adaptively weighted in prediction space, with magnitude- and direction-supervision targeting the remaining error. On the NREL-TSI benchmark, GateFormer attains 125.01 W/m^2 RMSE at +30 min, improving over a state-of-the-art transformer baseline by 9.6% under paired-timestamp evaluation. Across NREL-TSI, Chilbolton, and SIRTA, GateFormer achieves the lowest final-horizon RMSE among the evaluated baselines, with forecast skill of 22.97-28.86% relative to smart persistence. Component ablations show adaptive weighting outperforms both individual decoders and fixed averaging, distinguishing GateFormer from conventional forecast combination, while the supervised correction further reduces RMSE by 1.68 W/m^2 and MAE by 4.86 W/m^2. Ramp-regime diagnostics show larger gains during operationally important positive ramps, reducing RMSE by 26.27 W/m^2. These results identify forecast-space decomposition as an alternative forecasting formulation, with potential relevance to other multimodal short-horizon forecasting tasks and deployment using only sky images and measured GHI.

title: Sensorimotor Alignment: A Platonic Proxy for Embodied Policy Success
abstract: Robotic foundation models are typically evaluated through costly closed-loop rollouts, which motivates cheap offline proxies for model capability. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests that as representations improve, different modalities such as vision and language converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. We ask whether motion trajectories form another such modality: as embodied models become more capable, should their sensory representations converge toward the structure of physical motion? To examine this, we propose Sensorimotor Alignment ($S^2$), a training-free offline metric that measures how well a model's sensory representation aligns with the geometry of physical motion. We find that $S^2$ correlates positively with downstream robot task success across embodied model families, making it a low-cost offline proxy for prioritizing models before closed-loop evaluation. $S^2$ can also identify promising vision-language model (VLM) backbones even before costly fine-tuning into vision-language-action models (VLAs). Beyond this correlation, $S^2$ offers representation-level explanations for phenomena observed in VLAs and world action models (WAMs). With $S^2$, we extend PRH to embodied models and make sensorimotor alignment empirically measurable, offering insight into why an embodied model succeeds beyond its closed-loop success rate.

title: Inside-JEPA: From Prediction to Relational Grounding in Latent World Models
abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models in latent space, enabling efficient planning but leaving their states opaque. We introduce Inside-JEPA, which places relational channels for ordered entity pairs inside the JEPA latent state and shows that an inverse-dynamics loss can ground these channels without relation labels when its head reads them, either alone or as part of the full state. On Something-Something V2, latent prediction alone performs no better than a random relation head, while inverse-dynamics supervision that recovers actions from channel changes improves relational AUROC by .065-.103 across ten settings with annotated boxes, by .081 on RH20T robot episodes with held-out tasks, and by .050-.061 across five relations using off-the-shelf detection and tracking. An inverse head on entity latents decodes actions more accurately but barely improves relational grounding; shuffled labels, two label-free objectives, and action labels on only 5% of the pairs also fail to ground the channels. Given an action, predicted relational changes approach the quality of observed future relations (AUROC .599 vs .621). For one-step relational goals, a supervised readout of the 16 channels ranks the correct action among the top five of 65 in 43% of cases, compared with 24% for prediction-only latents and 17% for a frequency prior.

title: Making MLLM Latents Matter: Factor-Aware Predictive Learning for Cinematic Video Generation
abstract: Cinematic video generation requires both temporal inference from limited inputs (i.e., sparse rather than frame-by-frame guidance) and factor-aware control of character, scene, action, and camera. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer useful priors for both capabilities, but their representations are not automatically actionable for video generation: a Video Diffusion Transformer (DiT) may bypass them through native conditioning pathways, and using them does not ensure either factor-aware control or generation-compatible temporal prediction. We propose Factor-Aware Predictive Learning (FAPL), which establishes effective MLLM latent use as a shared prerequisite and then targets the two capabilities with complementary learning signals. First, latent-only generator grounding trains the DiT with a frozen MLLM and connector, strengthening the DiT's use of MLLM latents for generation. Second, for factor-aware control, paired videos specify a target-factor change and non-target preservation, and factor-span replacement trains the DiT to realize this relationship in its output. Third, for temporal inference, text-only and text-plus-complete-video observations share a video target, and the trained DiT is then frozen while the MLLM and connector are optimized through it. This final stage trains limited-input representations for generation while retaining complete-observation reconstruction as a complementary training mode. Extensive experiments demonstrate our consistently better performance on three cinematic video generation tasks (i.e., sparse-to-video, factor-aware editing, and multi-shot generation) over baselines and validate FAPL's contributions to MLLM feature use, temporal control, and factor coordination.

Third, for temporal inference, text-only and text-plus-complete-video observations share a video target, and the trained DiT is then frozen while the MLLM and connector are optimized through it. This final stage trains limited-input representations for generation while retaining complete-observation reconstruction as a complementary training mode. Extensive experiments demonstrate our consistently better performance on three cinematic video generation tasks (i.e., sparse-to-video, factor-aware editing, and multi-shot generation) over baselines and validate FAPL's contributions to MLLM feature use, temporal control, and factor coordination.

title: When More Metadata Misleads: Probing Field-Level Grounding in LLM-Generated Museum Descriptions
abstract: Metadata-conditioned generation is often framed as a data-to-text task in which additional input fields should improve grounding. Museum description generation challenges this assumption because catalogue records are heterogeneous, partially visual, and unevenly documented across geographic regions. We study how metadata composition shapes the generation of artefact descriptions through a two-phase framework. Phase 1 analyses natural metadata variation in a large museum collection, where field count, field type, image availability, and Place co-vary. Phase 2 introduces controlled field probes that hold object identity fixed while varying metadata quantity, field type, and image access. Our results show that metadata quantity alone does not explain generation behaviour. Field type determines whether models ground, omit, or infer information, while images can both support visual grounding and increase unsupported interpretation. More broadly, our findings show that metadata-conditioned data-to-text evaluation should assess field- and claim-level support, rather than relying only on aggregate input coverage or reference similarity.

title: Inherited, Not Invented: Tracing the Provenance of Wait in Reasoning Models
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is credited with teaching reasoning models to write {wait} before reconsidering a step, yet large RL accuracy gains do not require the word. This view can confuse what RL discovers with what a model inherits from its training data. We trace the word through open models' training histories, reading it with label-free indices of frequency, position, form and usage and an injected-error test, all computed from sampled outputs. We find that zero-RL almost never coins the marker: on bases that lack the word, RL raises MATH-500 accuracy substantially while {wait} stays near absent. It arrives with training data: mid-training in OLMo-3, and fine-tuning on reasoning traces installs it in most models whose base lacks it. Where the base already uses it, both released RL-Zero recipes (OLMo-3, MiMo) multiply it, whereas KL-free GRPO from the same base does not; OLMo-3's recipe wears down its form and makes it a more sensitive but more liberal alarm; RL after supervised fine-tuning barely changes it, and our GRPO recipe erases a marker seeded by fine-tuning. Finally, we show that marker frequency alone does not indicate RL-induced reasoning and caution against LLM-as-a-judge revision metrics, as automated judges can reverse human-labelled trends.

title: Direct Pass@$k$ Optimization for Thought Pruning: Balancing Quality and Diversity in Test-Time Reasoning
abstract: Test-time scaling has emerged as a key inference strategy for reasoning models, where a model generates a large number of candidate solutions in the hope of finding at least one correct solution. Running all candidate solutions to completion can be computationally demanding, so recent work prunes the candidate pool after generating only a short prefix, committing further computation only to the surviving candidates. Existing pruning strategies divide broadly into two categories: Quality-based methods assign a score to each partial solution and discard those predicted to ultimately lead to an incorrect final solution, while diversity-based methods select partial solutions that follow different reasoning trajectories and are therefore likely to cover different final solutions. The tension between these two objectives is an instance of exploration versus exploitation, yet little to no prior work on pruning exposes this trade-off directly, let alone optimizes it. In this paper, we introduce a pruning procedure that addresses this trade-off directly by optimizing pass@$k$ over the selected solution pool. In particular, it chooses the pool to maximize the probability that at least one of its partial solutions, when continued to completion, yields a correct answer. Because this objective simultaneously rewards high-quality partial solutions and penalizes redundancy among them, quality and diversity are naturally balanced by the criterion itself rather than through separate ad-hoc design choices. On eight open-weight reasoning models, our method outperforms existing quality-based and diversity-based pruning strategies. The gains are particularly pronounced when the pruning procedure keeps a moderate number of partial solutions for continued generation, highlighting the value of directly balancing quality and diversity during pruning.

title: RaSFNet: Ray-aligned and Scan-aware Fusion Network for LiDAR Semantic Segmentation
abstract: LiDAR point cloud semantic segmentation is a fundamental component of 3D perception for autonomous driving and robotics. Projection-based methods map 3D point clouds into 2D representations for feature extraction using 2D networks. However, aggregating multiple points during projection can obscure geometric differences within each frustum, while local feature extraction limits the modeling of spatial relationships across scanning regions. Moreover, proximity in the projected representation does not necessarily imply proximity in 3D space, and interactions between point and projected features may mix features from different ranges, reducing semantic discriminability. To address these challenges, we propose the Ray-aligned and Scan-aware Fusion Network (RaSFNet), which incorporates point cloud geometry and LiDAR scanning characteristics into projection-based semantic segmentation. Specifically, the Ray-Aligned Geometric Distribution Encoding (RAGDE) module characterizes point distributions within each frustum using a ray-aligned coordinate system. To model spatial context, a Scan-Topology-Aware Mamba (STAM) block organizes frustum features according to the LiDAR azimuth sampling pattern and captures long-range dependencies across scanning regions. In addition, a Range-Constrained Point-Frustum Fusion (RCPFF) mechanism uses shared range information to guide feature exchange between point and frustum representations while maintaining spatial correspondence. RaSFNet achieves mIoU scores of 70.2% and 77.7% on the SemanticKITTI and nuScenes validation sets, respectively, indicating competitive segmentation performance compared with the evaluated methods.

title: Phase Transition from Random Features to Fully Trainable Networks
abstract: Constructing accurate and computationally tractable approximation spaces is a fundamental task in scientific computing. Partially trainable neural networks bridge fixed random features and fully adaptive representations. This paper quantifies a phase transition pattern in approximation bounds and observes analogous behavior in training errors: a rapid but smooth initial improvement followed by diminishing returns, with a sharper transition under greater initialization mismatch. Under polynomial spectral decay with exponent $α>1$ and leverage compatibility, we establish a squared $L_2$ approximation rate $\mathcal{O}((κ_P\log(m/δ)/m)^α)$ for two-layer networks of width $m$ and trainable proportion $P$, where $κ_P=(P/κ_1^*+(1-P)/κ_0^*)^{-1}$. The bound holds uniformly over the unit ball of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) with probability at least $1-δ$. The constants $κ_0^*$ and $κ_1^*$ quantify the fixed and trainable groups' sampling mismatches relative to the target RKHS. For spherical biased-ReLU features in dimension $d$, we verify these assumptions with $α=(d+2)/(d-1)$ and $κ_0^*=4\sqrt{2}τ(d+1)/d$ for initialization scale $τ\ge1$, and $κ_1^*=1$ under ridge leverage sampling. For $d=5$ and $τ=10$, a trainable proportion of approximately $4.1\%$ captures $90\%$ of the reduction in the approximation bound from $P=0$ to $P=1$. A structured three-layer example illustrates how a few trainable first-layer neurons exploit fixed downstream blocks through nonlinear composition. Numerical experiments across diverse settings, including networks with up to 15 layers, exhibit similar phase transitions in training errors.

title: Track finding and particle identification performance with particle physics foundation models
abstract: Modern high energy nuclear and particle physics experiments produce large amounts of sparse data that must be reduced significantly in size before performing physics analysis. Recently, there has been an effort to evaluate Foundation Models as a potential tool for performing data analysis. These models have been shown to learn features in high dimensional datasets based on the multi-modal data they are trained on. To show their effectiveness at performing complex pattern recognition tasks, such as reconstructing charged particles in a magnetic field, we evaluated the performance of a Foundation Model based reconstruction on several downstream tasks with a dataset composed of spacepoints in a Time Projection Chamber. We show that the performance of the Foundation Model based data analysis significantly improves upon that of traditional methods, and furthermore can be adapted to learn additional tasks that are not necessarily related to the initial training objective.
