title: De-identification of child protection intake reports using relationship-based replacement (DI-REBAR)
abstract: Background Child protection contacts are documented in the form of child protection intake reports detailing the child(ren) suspected to be at risk of harm, the notifier's concerns, the alleged person responsible, and other details. These narrative reports remain untapped for statistical reporting and research purposes due to being text-based as well as containing extremely sensitive content. Applying a contextual de-identification approach to child protection narratives opens up the possibility of large-scale automated analysis by external researchers while preserving data privacy and relational meaning. Data 10,000 randomly selected South Australian Department for Child Protection intake reports were provided for this study. A total of 300 (200 development, 100 evaluation) were randomly selected, manually reviewed and annotated. Methods We designed and implemented a context-preserving de-identification pipeline called De-Identification via Relationship-Based Replacement (DI-REBAR) on 10,000 reports while preserving the noted relationships between named individuals. A total of seven indirect identifiers (date, time, school, early learning centre, hospital, prison, sensitive reference numbers) and three direct identifiers (name, address, phone number) were selected for de-identification. A relationship table was temporarily created to map individuals and their relationship to the child of interest, with direct identifiers replaced. Indirect identifiers were replaced by list-based replacement and regular expressions. Results DI-REBAR evaluation showed promising results in macro precision (>0.98), recall (>0.88), and F1-Score (>0.92) across nine out of the ten identifier classes (prison excluded). Each identifier had a range of precision (0.74-1.00), recall (0.61-1.00), and F1-Score (0.66-1.00). Address, phone number, and date have the best performances (>0.98) across precision, recall, and F1-Score. Conclusion This is the first Australian study to automatically de-identify sensitive child protection data whilst preserving relationship information, allowing large-scale text analysis by external researchers in a data custodian's controlled environment. This approach can be applied to other areas that rely on unstructured data such as court documents and police reports. However, human reviewers are still needed to ensure identifiable information is not disclosed.

title: SABLE: Scalable Affine Bayesian Latent-space Exploration
abstract: Complex objects such as engineering designs and proteins are often difficult to optimise because their design spaces exhibit high-dimensional structure and objective evaluations are expensive. Generative models provide continuous latent representations, but their latent spaces can have thousands to tens of thousands of dimensions, creating a regime where the latent dimension $D$ greatly exceeds the evaluation budget. We introduce SABLE, a Bayesian optimisation method for high-dimensional latent spaces with an isotropic distribution and limited budget. SABLE uses a Bayesian affine surrogate for prediction and acquisition, treating higher-order structure as surrogate discrepancy. After $N$ observations, the slope update has dimension at most $N-1$, yielding a decomposition of each query into an in-span component optimised by expected improvement (EI) in at most $N$ dimensions and an off-span component governed by a scalar norm. We show that the off-span norm implicitly selected by affine EI can lead to underexploration, and SABLE instead prescribes it using a finite-horizon schedule, without restricting search to a learned subspace. A recompression scheme reduces information to $\mathcal O(M)$ pseudo-observations, bounding refitting cost by $\mathcal O(M^2D+M^3)$ while keeping parameter inference, prediction, and acquisition decisions to tens of milliseconds. Across synthetic benchmarks and latent-space optimisation tasks, SABLE achieves high sample efficiency and reduces decision time by several orders of magnitude at large budgets.

title: Revisiting Distribution Matching for State-to-Vision Policy Distillation in Laparoscopic Robotic Manipulation
abstract: End-to-end control policies trained via Reinforcement Learning (RL) have emerged as an alternative to conventional surgical robotic control approaches, with recent studies exploring state-based policies trained on privileged state observations. However, such approaches rely on precise physical states that are difficult to obtain reliably in surgical environments. Vision-based RL provides an alternative by learning manipulation policies directly from RGB observations, avoiding explicit state estimation and manually engineered perception pipelines while enabling policies to acquire task-relevant visual representations. Nevertheless, obtaining vision-based policies via pure RL methods for surgical manipulation remains challenging. Thus, imitation learning (IL) becomes another solution, yet it requires a large number of expert demonstrations, which are difficult to obtain in minimally invasive surgery. In this work, we propose a framework for state-to-vision policy distillation in laparoscopic robotic manipulation. Specifically, a state-based policy with privileged observations is employed as the teacher, and a vision-based policy learns from RGB observations and robot proprioceptive information, which requires less expert demonstrations than IL and introduces superior performance than RL methods. We conduct extensive experiments on various surgical manipulation tasks in the simulated environment. Experimental results show that, in the context of laparoscopic robotic manipulation, training vision-based policies with general-purpose RL methods is challenging, whereas our proposed state-to-vision policy distillation leads to more consistent and stable performance across tasks.

title: Mitigating Saliency Collapse: Robust Saliency-Aware Long-Text Image-Text Alignment
abstract: Long-text image-text alignment is essential for fine-grained scene understanding, yet existing methods mainly focus on extending context length or improving local alignment. We identify an overlooked failure mode, saliency collapse, where models over-rely on text that features visual prominence while underutilizing non-salient context. Consequently, retrieval performance degrades sharply when salient content is reduced, despite that the non-salient context remains informative. To address this, we propose RoSA, a saliency-aware finetuning framework that decomposes image-text pairs into complementary salient and contextual views, enabling joint learning of prominent and contextual semantics. We propose a modality-independent decomposition strategy to combine object-level visual saliency estimation with LLM-based text decomposition to bridge vision and language. We employ auxiliary objectives to explicitly align these views, ensuring robust representation with both salient and contextual features. RoSA greatly improves long-text retrieval and demonstrates strong robustness to saliency collapse across benchmarks. Moreover, our auxiliary objectives are plug-and-play, bringing consistent gains to existing tuning methods. Code and checkpoints are available at: https://github.com/intelligolabs/RoSA

title: A Gaussian Mixture Model for Multiple Instance Learning With Both Bag‐ and Instance‐Level Features
abstract: ABSTRACT The core challenge of multiple instance learning (MIL) is to predict bag‐level labels with partially or completely unobserved instance‐level labels. Most existing methods focus on instance‐level features and ignore commonly available bag‐level covariates. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel Gaussian mixture model (GMM) framework that fuses both bag‐ and instance‐level features. The framework introduces an instance‐level background class to characterize instances weakly related to the target topic. It models the two types of features with separate Gaussian distributions and fuses cross‐level information by combining the bag‐level label distribution with the conditional distribution of instance‐level labels. evidence.title: A Gaussian Mixture Model for Multiple Instance Learning With Both Bag‐ and Instance‐Level Features
evidence.abstract: ABSTRACT The core challenge of multiple instance learning (MIL) is to predict bag‐level labels with partially or completely unobserved instance‐level labels. Most existing methods focus on instance‐level features and ignore commonly available bag‐level covariates. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel Gaussian mixture model (GMM) framework that fuses both bag‐ and instance‐level features. The framework introduces an instance‐level background class to characterize instances weakly related to the target topic. It models the two types of features with separate Gaussian distributions and fuses cross‐level information by combining the bag‐level label distribution with the conditional distribution of instance‐level labels. For parameter estimation, a two‐step strategy is adopted: Bag‐level parameters are obtained in closed form, while instance‐level parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood via the EM algorithm. Numerical simulations verify the consistency of the proposed estimator, and the proposed method achieves substantially higher prediction accuracy than the baseline GMM (using only single‐level features) and classical MIL methods. title: Self-Supervised Multibeam Sonar Restoration via Coherent Forward Modeling
abstract: Multibeam imaging sonar produces intensity images degraded by coherent speckle and system-induced blur, while clean reflectivity targets are rarely available. Existing despeckling methods often rely on simplified intensity-domain noise models, synthetic clean targets, or blind-spot self-supervision, and typically do not jointly model deblurring and speckle suppression. We propose a physics-consistent self-supervised framework for joint despeckling and deblurring of multibeam imaging sonar. A stochastic coherent image-formation model yields a conditional-mean forward operator that relates latent scene reflectivity to expected intensity through the squared magnitude of the system point spread function. We then use registered multi-frame sonar sequences to train without clean ground truth images, showing that, under an idealized inter-frame conditional-mean condition, the expected paired loss equals the corresponding forward-prediction loss up to a network-independent constant. To stabilize the ill-conditioned inverse problem, we further adapt robust equivariant imaging using stochastic coherent simulation and introduce a paired forward prediction error metric for ground-truth-free evaluation. Experiments on two real multibeam sonar datasets demonstrate a favourable balance between forward-prediction agreement, homogeneous-region speckle suppression, and preservation of visible structural boundaries compared with representative baselines.

title: Agri-SCHOLAR: Simulation-Grounded In-Season Rolling Advisories for Agricultural Crops Using LLM-Bounded Optimization
abstract: Existing agricultural advisories to farmers suffer from several limitations: (a) remain largely expert-driven, (b) do not adequately account for in-season weather, and (c) do not scale to individual farms. In this paper, our objective is to close these gaps by developing Agri-SCHOLAR (Simulation-Grounded Crop Harvest Optimization with LLM-Guided In-Season Advisory Rollouts). Agri-SCHOLAR is a rolling, in-season advisory framework that issues, at intervals of every few days or every week, a personalized advisory using the following information: soil and crop properties, observed weather to date, short-range forecast of weather, and a season extrapolation of weather based on historical analogs. The novelty and depth of Agri-SCHOLAR lies in each advisory being produced by a closed-loop system which couples multiple LLM agents with a powerful crop simulator (such as APSIM in our case). The simulator crucially serves as an evaluation oracle. In Agri-SCHOLAR, the LLM agents propose agronomically sound and feasible bounds on actionable parameters and an optimizer searches within those bounds against a multi-objective reward spanning yield, resource utilization, and economic feasibility. We conduct a detailed 11-year analysis of the maize crop in two selected locations of South Asia and show that Agri-SCHOLAR consistently outperforms the region's standard packages of practice and satisfactorily addresses the limitations of existing agricultural advisories.

title: Training Small Language Models for Transferable Tool Selection
abstract: As LLM agents operate over corpora of more than ten thousand tools, selecting the right tool for a complex multi-step user instruction becomes a central bottleneck. Tool descriptions cannot all fit in context, and relevance-based retrievers only rank tools without knowing which are actually needed. Recent work instead leverages proprietary commercial LLMs like Claude or ChatGPT to drive a retriever, decomposing the instruction and selecting over retrieved candidates. We show that a small, open model can be trained via reinforcement learning to perform the same functionality. On ToolBench, a Qwen3-8B model post-trained with our recipe outperforms Llama-4-Maverick (402B). In addition, the trained model transfers directly to different retrievers and generalizes to new tool corpora in different domains.

title: SecLog-Bench: A Scalable Benchmark for Cybersecurity Log Reasoning with Scaffolded Evidence
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for cybersecurity, leading to growing interest in LLM-based automated cybersecurity log analysis. However, current datasets (1) are limited in scale; (2) rely mainly on single-source evidence; and (3) have only binary or multi-class attack labels, without dense annotations of the reasoning process. To address these limitations, SecLog-Bench has three key features. First, we build an extensible simulation platform that covers 29 attack scenarios, supports repeated execution and the integration of new scenarios, and enables scalable generation of cybersecurity logs with attack-stage labels. Second, we use multi-source logs, including audit logs, application logs, and network traffic, to jointly analyze cyber attacks. Third, we annotate each sample with the essential context for cybersecurity log reasoning and a structured step-by-step evidence chain. We evaluate eight mainstream LLMs on this benchmark for post-detection attack-progress reasoning. Results show that, when provided with scaffolded evidence, current LLMs exhibit modest capability in attack-progress reasoning, with the best model achieving only 44.44% accuracy and 45.07% Macro-F1. Their reasoning remains unreliable; i.e., the highest Stage Reasoning F1 (SRF1) score is only 54.87%. Moreover, even correct predictions may be accompanied by flawed reasoning, and reasoning quality is often misaligned with prediction accuracy.

title: Deep learning-based mitotic quantification for objective adjunct for grading of urothelial carcinoma: a multi-institutional validation study
abstract: Abstract Histological grading of urothelial carcinoma is subject to interobserver variability. We evaluated whether artificial intelligence (AI)-based whole-slide mitotic quantification provides an objective adjunct to histological grading. We developed and validated a deep learning-based mitotic detection framework trained on 91,183 patches with 318,893 annotations. A multi-reader crossover study was conducted in internal ( n = 149) and external ( n = 316) cohorts, where three independent pathologists graded cases in unassisted and model-assisted phases. In the combined cohort ( n = 465), AI-derived mitotic count showed high diagnostic accuracy for high-grade carcinoma (area under the curve [AUC] 0.91, 95% CI 0.89–0.94) at a cut-off of 17.5 mitoses per 2 mm². AI assistance significantly improved mean reader AUC from 0.90 to 0.98 in the internal cohort ( p = 0.038). In the external cohort, the mean reader AUC increased from 0.84 to 0.95, although this difference did not reach statistical significance ( p = 0.11). AI assistance also significantly reduced interobserver variability (Fleiss’s κ: 0.72 to 0.93 internally; 0.62 to 0.85 externally; both, p < 0.001). AI-based mitotic quantification provides an objective and standardized adjunct to histological grading and reduces interobserver variability. This approach may improve diagnostic accuracy and support clinical decision-making, pending prospective validation.

title: Evaluating the Applicability of LLM Inference Optimizations on Apple Silicon
abstract: Apple Silicon is among the most widely used platforms for local LLM inference, yet nearly all inference optimizations are designed and validated on server-class NVIDIA GPUs under batched serving workloads. Which optimizations retain their benefits when moved to Apple Silicon, and what determines their applicability? We evaluate four optimization families: KV-cache pruning, speculative decoding, ported GPU kernels, and post-training quantization. Experiments span four Apple machines under a common single-request decode workload, with matched RTX 4090 comparisons where possible. KV-cache pruning can reach up to 1.75 times end-to-end throughput on Apple but can reduce throughput on desktop NVIDIA GPUs. Under the common benchmark, all evaluated speculative decoding methods reduce throughput on Apple, despite reported 2-6 times gains on server GPUs. CUDA kernel designs transfer only partially: public Metal lacks asynchronous copy, and batch-one decode makes several serving-oriented mechanisms inapplicable, although transferable components yield up to 1.20 times decode throughput. Quantization gains vary by machine. Across four families, a reported speedup is not a portable property of a technique alone but a joint function of technique, runtime, hardware contract, and workload regime.

title: Truthful by Omission: Click Thinning for LLM-Native Advertising
abstract: Generative AI assistants are becoming an advertising medium, embedding sponsored content in their answers. This setting departs from classical position auctions in two ways: an ad's click-through rate depends on the passage that hosts it, and because users stop at their first click, earlier ads take clicks from later ones. This competition for clicks makes truthfulness delicate: a higher bid can reshape the allocation and put a competitor ahead of the bidder, reducing the bidder's clicks. Existing mechanisms either attain a constant fraction of the optimal welfare (advertisers' total click value) but are not known to be truthful, or are truthful but their welfare guarantee degrades as the number of passages grows. We achieve both even when the answer and its editorial order are fixed before bidding. Assuming each ad's click-through rate when reached is known and unaffected by omitting other ads, we give a computationally efficient mechanism that is truthful in expectation and attains at least half the optimal welfare under free reordering. Our key idea, click thinning, omits ads at random, showing earlier ads less often so that each ad's overall click probability no longer depends on the order of the ads. Welfare maximization then reduces to a tractable matching problem, and solving it exactly with VCG-style payments makes truthful bidding optimal in expectation. Characterizing the click probabilities that omission can achieve sharpens the approximation factor from $2$ to $2-(1-δ)^{K-1}$ when at most $K$ ads are shown and each click-through rate is at most $δ$. This factor is the best possible for any order-preserving rule, even one that ignores incentives and computation, so truthfulness and computational efficiency incur no additional worst-case loss.

title: Trait or Bias? Why item keying is indispensable when comparing language model responses across languages
abstract: Cross-linguistic differences in large language model (LLM) questionnaire responses are increasingly interpreted as evidence of culturally patterned behaviour. Such inferences, however, assume that observed score differences reflect variation in the target construct rather than artefacts of measurement. The present study examines this assumption using three established Likert measures of social orientation administered in English and Chinese to four contemporary LLMs. Leveraging balanced-keying scales, we decompose observed cross-linguistic differences into a trait-related component and a response-bias component associated with item keying. We further test the role of item wording through keying manipulations that preserve substantive content while altering item direction. Across models and instruments, the observed language effect was found to comprise two separable components of comparable magnitude but opposite sign. The bias component was highly consistent, with English prompting producing greater agreement tendencies than Chinese prompting in every balanced-keying condition. Rewording experiments showed that the effect tracked item wording rather than substantive content, while analyses of forward-keyed instruments indicated that the two components were confounded in conventional scores. As a consequence, identical composite scores could arise from different combinations of trait-related variation and response bias. These findings do not challenge the existence of cross-linguistic variation in LLM responses. Rather, they challenge the interpretation of observed score differences as direct indicators of underlying cultural orientation. The results suggest that cross-linguistic differences in questionnaire responses reflect both construct-related variation and language-dependent response tendencies, and that balanced-keying designs are necessary to distinguish between them. More broadly, the study highlights the importance of measurement validity in cross-linguistic evaluations of LLMs and argues that prompt language should be treated as a substantive measurement variable rather than a neutral medium of expression.

title: All‐Optical Dual‐Angle Diffractive Neural Networks for 2D Direction‐of‐Arrival Estimation
abstract: ABSTRACT Accurate direction‐of‐arrival (DoA) estimation in real time is essential for stable terahertz (THz) communications. To overcome the limitations of previous diffractive methods that are restricted to 1D sensing or depend on rotation, and to advance their practical deployment, we propose and experimentally validate an all‐optical dual‐angle diffractive neural network (DA‐DNN) capable of simultaneous 2D angular classification. At the heart of our design is a diffractive aperture placed before the neural network as a physical encoder. It converts the phase‐only angular information carried by the incident wave into a complex optical field enriched with amplitude features, thereby producing robust spatial encoding sensitive to angle. The system is modeled using the Rayleigh–Sommerfeld diffraction integral and optimized through end‐to‐end backpropagation. We fabricate a compact, monolithically integrated DA‐DNN device using 3D printing at high resolution and evaluate it through full‐wave simulations and THz experiments that emulate communication environments. The system accurately recognizes 64 angular combinations over a range, providing a passive and scalable optical solution with low latency for THz communications.

title: MoG-VLM: Efficient Video Anomaly Detection through Motion-Guided Vision-Language Models
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have shown strong potential for video anomaly detection, but dense frame-level inference makes them impractical for real-time deployment. Existing acceleration commonly relies on uniform sampling, which ignores content dynamics and can either waste computation on static segments or miss localized anomalies. We propose MoG-VLM a motion-adaptive anomaly detection framework that leverages motion purely as a lightweight control signal to decide when VLM inference is necessary. To this end, we introduce Temporal Gradient Magnitude (TGM) which performs content-aware sampling to concentrate computation on informative regions while avoiding redundant processing. We further introduce a hierarchical dual-stream design in which dense multi-frame VLM reasoning is activated only around frames with elevated anomaly likelihood, via anchor-triggered context-window expansion with early termination. A fusion module then reconciles these instantaneous semantic cues with temporal action dynamics. Across four benchmarks, our method achieves 91.91%, 84.30%, 87.88%, and 78.96% AUC-ROC on XD-Violence, UCF-Crime, MSAD, and ShanghaiTech, respectively, establishing new state of the art on three benchmarks under the zero-shot, training-free setting. On XD-Violence, we improve over the previous best result by +0.57% while delivering a 1.31x inference speedup. These results demonstrate that content-aware allocation of VLM capacity, processing fewer frames more intelligently rather than all frames uniformly, is a more effective axis of progress than uniformly densifying VLM inference across frames. Code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/kdawoud91/MoG-VLM.

title: Platonic Projection Structures-Based Information Dynamics (PPS-ID): Recursive Transformation of Observable Information
abstract: In recursive learning, model outputs can be reused in subsequent training, linking successive models through the reuse and transformation of observable information. Assessing these processes requires distinguishing changes in observable states from the preservation of task-relevant properties. We introduce PPS-Based Information Dynamics (PPS-ID), a framework connecting the observability perspective of Platonic Projection Structures with trajectory-based evaluation of repeated learning. PPS-ID separates latent-to-observable mappings from training-state transitions and evaluates observable discrepancies, task-dependent directional variation, and example-level correctness histories. Standard factorization conditions specify when the chosen observations admit a closed transition, while decision-margin conditions relate changes in prediction probabilities to preservation of classification decisions. Experiments with CIFAR-10 and sentiment classification using Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) illustrate three distinctions: local similarity can coexist with departure from an initial state; accuracy decline can coexist with lower expected calibration error and higher prediction entropy; and endpoint improvement can coexist with intermediate losses. In five-generation CIFAR-10 distillation across five seeds, fixed-teacher final accuracy exceeds recursive final accuracy by a mean of 1.542 percentage points under soft-only supervision. Mixing ground-truth and soft-target supervision reverses this ranking and raises mean recursive final accuracy from 70.672% to 73.910%. On the binary Stanford Sentiment Treebank task (SST-2) and IMDb, BERT experiments yield dataset- and seed-dependent endpoint rankings; first-generation branch differences limit causal attribution to teacher replacement. PPS-ID provides a common evaluation structure for examining how observable information changes and which task-relevant properties are preserved along a learning trajectory. The results show how supervision regime, reference choice, and intermediate variation affect the interpretation of repeated learning.

title: Ask About the Right Moment: Training-Free Object Identity Reasoning for Video-Language Models
abstract: Many questions about a video concern one physical object. Where does the ball end up after the cups are shuffled? Which card is the queen? How often was the mug covered? Video-language models (Video-LMs) recognise such objects in single frames but do not keep them apart over time. On real shell-game videos, open models from 8B to 235B parameters, their thinking variants, a reinforcement-learned tool agent and three training-free tool agents all stay within ten points of chance. We separate semantic identity binding from temporal identity maintenance. An object's identity should be fixed at a moment when the evidence for it is visible, and carried afterwards by a tracker. \emph{Track, Then Bind} implements this principle without training. A promptable video tracker follows every candidate object and draws it with a track number. A frozen vision-language model answers a static question about the identifying evidence, which binds the target to a track. The answer is then derived from the tracked state in text, without asking the model to reinterpret the original video during read-out. A single configuration covers all benchmarks. With Qwen3-VL-32B it solves both VET-Bench tasks, where a fine-tuned trajectory model reaches 92\% and 90\% and the same VLM voting over 16 samples stays at 30--32\%. It answers 55.4\% of the hardest Perception Test cup games, where the best published model answers 41.5\%, and, using track-derived timelines, 48.6\% of TOC-Bench questions, against 37.1\% for the same model answering directly. Drawing the same tracks on the video and asking the question directly falls 12--19 points short of the agent on real cup games.

title: EEG-Captioner: Grounding EEG-to-Language Generation in Fundamental Signal Properties
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG)-to-language models offer a promising approach for translating complex neural signals into human-readable descriptions. However, generating plausible language does not necessarily demonstrate that a model has learned to interpret the underlying EEG signal. A direct way to assess such interpretation is to probe objectively measurable properties of the signal itself. We therefore construct an EEG-language dataset of 160,781 segments annotated with signal-level question answering (QA) pairs, where each question targets one of five property families and requires a quantitative comparison involving spectral, spatial, temporal, or lateral signal properties. Each segment is also paired with a feature-grounded EEG caption. We further propose a Dual-Domain EEG Encoder that jointly models temporal waveforms and spectral-spatial representations, and introduce EEG-Captioner, a unified EEG-to-language framework trained with both signal-level QA and EEG caption supervision. Experiments show that the proposed encoder achieves the highest overall macro-averaged balanced accuracy (Macro-BA) among the compared EEG encoders, while EEG-Captioner achieves a Macro-BA of 88.81% on signal-level QA and improves caption factual consistency from 82.06% to 83.46% over caption-only language adaptation, demonstrating the complementary benefits of signal-level QA and caption supervision.

title: Measuring the Verifier's Floor: How Much Apparent Rare-Word Text-to-Speech Error Is ASR Error?
abstract: Text-to-speech (TTS) is usually evaluated by transcribing its output with an automatic speech recognition (ASR) system, so the word error rate also counts recognizer errors. We measure these errors on human recordings of the test sentences. On LibriSpeech and FLEURS, the evaluation recognizer misses 33-67% of very rare words even in human speech, and all three recognizers miss 22-42%. Checking every word with two more recognizer families lowers the apparent TTS error on words that at least one recognizer hears two- to three-fold (very rare LibriSpeech words: from 10-13% to 3-5%), yet very rare words remain the hardest. Ignoring words the recognizer misses in human speech is biased: the other recognizers find TTS errors far more often on these words (4-6% vs. 0.2-0.3%) and overturn about half of the errors this mask keeps. As half of the remaining adjudicated errors may be spelling variants, a listening test is needed.

title: ColaBench: Evaluating Memory-Guided Knowledge Acquisition in Personal Agents
abstract: Personal agents need to draw on long-term interaction history to retrieve and apply external knowledge suited to a user's current request. Even an answer grounded in relevant documents can be unsuitable when it overlooks the user's circumstances. This creates two connected challenges: using historical conditions to identify the knowledge needed for a new request, and applying that knowledge to the user's situation. Existing benchmarks advance memory recall, personalized retrieval, and memory-guided action, while the joint evaluation of these two challenges remains underexplored. We introduce ColaBench, a synthetic benchmark in health and daily living, with 349 tasks across 10 Profiles and a knowledge base of 13,033 documents. Its Evidence Graph connects personal conditions to their disclosures across public interaction sessions, records prior document exposure, and links answer requirements to personal and newly acquired document evidence. We also introduce MemKB, which uses state summaries to inform queries and rule application, and memory-document links to retrieve knowledge associated with the user's history. MemKB achieves 86.25% Accuracy with an average of 4.07 interaction rounds per task. Task-level analysis finds larger gains on tasks integrating information across multiple historical Facts; error analysis further identifies unsupported personal assumptions and rule misapplication as obstacles to using retrieved evidence. ColaBench provides traceable tasks and an evaluation framework for studying how memory guides knowledge acquisition and rule application.

title: 4Cast Lab: Open-Source App for Machine Learning & Statistical Analysis
abstract: 4Cast Lab is a free, open-source application for machine learning, econometrics and statistical analysis that runs on the user's own computer, with no installation, no programming and no data leaving the machine. It was developed at the E|M|E|F Lab, Department of Economics, Democritus University of Thrace, for researchers, analysts, instructors and students in any field. Its Forecasting mode trains eight learning algorithms (with three kernels for SVM/SVR), implemented from scratch, under leakage-safe validation for time-ordered data; it selects models by cross-validation, compares the selected model with every alternative and with naive benchmarks through formal tests of predictive accuracy, and documents each run in a methods report and a Python script that the user can export. Its Estimation mode covers the core of applied econometrics, from OLS with robust inference to ARIMA, ARDL, VAR/VECM and GARCH. This paper describes the design, the interface and the workflow of version 4.6.2, reports a validation of 1,234 numerical results against statsmodels, linearmodels, arch, scikit-learn and NIST certified values, illustrates the workflow with three examples, and discusses current limitations.

title: Learning global and local representations for generalized category discovery in neurodegenerative diseases
abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) has achieved notable success in closed‐set classification of neurodegenerative diseases, but its performance degrades significantly in more realistic open‐set settings, such as discovering rare or novel disease subtypes from unlabeled data that are not seen during training. Purpose This study introduces, to our knowledge, the first framework for generalized category discovery (GCD) in neurodegenerative diseases using MRI. It aims to leverage labeled data from known categories to automatically identify novel categories within unlabeled datasets. Methods We propose a GCD framework integrating semi‐supervised contrastive learning with global‐local representation learning to jointly optimize feature learning. Globally, we enforce consistency between weakly augmented views of the same instance by aligning their similarity relationships with other embeddings in a support queue. Locally, we treat neighborhood embeddings from the support queue as positive pairs for cross‐instance contrastive learning, enhancing fine‐grained discrimination. This dual strategy results in a unified learning objective that is applicable to both labeled and unlabeled data, effectively narrowing the representation gap among semantically similar instances. Results We evaluate our method on a benchmark dataset comprising six neurodegenerative diseases, with over 1500 patient samples. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms representative state‐of‐the‐art methods. Specifically, our method achieves 66.02% Accuracy and 60.59% Normalized Mutual Information on all categories, and 54.53% Accuracy and 16.67% Normalized Mutual Information on novel categories, surpassing existing state‐of‐the‐art methods. Conclusions Our framework underscores the model's robustness and its practical value in discovering new neurodegenerative disease conditions, highlighting its potential for advancing open‐set diagnostic AI.

title: From Structured Records to Patient Narratives: Preserving Clinical Alignment in LLM-Generated Health Summaries
abstract: As wearable and digital health systems increasingly generate longitudinal physiological records, communicating these observations in patient-accessible language remains a significant challenge. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising mechanism for translating structured clinical information into readable narratives, but this process may introduce semantic drift, where clinically precise meaning is distorted during simplification. We investigate evidence-grounded health summarization for menstrual health monitoring using a constrained generation framework that combines structured evidence conditioning with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) using a prompt-based constrained generation framework. We evaluate semantic alignment using Natural Language Inference (NLI), atomic factuality metrics, and readability measures. Across three LLMs and 4,500 generated summaries, explicit grounding constraints consistently improve clinical alignment, particularly by improving uncertainty preservation and, once faithfulness is evaluated against retrieved evidence, generally preserving or improving faithfulness, while effects on omission remain model-dependent. We also find that improved clinical alignment comes at the cost of increased reading difficulty and medical terminology. These findings highlight the need to jointly evaluate faithfulness, uncertainty preservation, and readability when developing patient-facing medical LLM systems.

title: Interpretive Variation and Discourse Structure in Detecting Enthymemes in Controversial Political Discourse
abstract: Enthymemes are arguments that leave a premise or conclusion unstated, and they are a common persuasion device on social media. Because readers must fill in the missing part themselves, they often disagree on whether a text contains one. This paper asks how to detect and evaluate enthymemes when such disagreement is part of the task. On tweets about vaccination and immigration, each labeled by five annotators, F1 stalls around 0.67 for every fine-tuned model we train, regardless of data size, added features or label type. We therefore ask how these models should be evaluated instead, and propose metrics that compare predictions with the full distribution of annotator votes, together with a model that predicts this distribution directly and captures disagreement better at no cost in F1. We then ask what role discourse structure plays. Models learn to rely on explicit argumentative structure: they reliably recognize tweets without an enthymeme but rarely commit on tweets that contain one. Both the models and a discourse parser miss arguments whose links are left implicit and must be inferred by the reader. Finally, we discuss what these blind spots mean for content moderation systems trained on majority labels.

title: Efficiënte ontwerpmethoden voor kostenefficiënte maskering: afwegingen bij zijkanaalbeveiliging in hardware
abstract: The main goal of the research is to contribute to countermeasures to protect hardware implementations of symmetric cryptographic algorithms against physical attacks. It can include both countermeasures against passive and active attacks. The research is aimed to study such concepts as masking, threshold implementations, randomness generation and many others in order to improve the security and performance of the hardware implementations against a more realistic adversary model. This contribution can help to define metrics for combined security and to develop procedures for their evaluation in the future.

title: Temporal Naive Bayes: an efficient probabilistic framework for real-time maneuver recognition and anomaly monitoring in autonomous driving
abstract: The capacity to anticipate and identify anomalous behavior remains fundamental to the safety and operational reliability of autonomous mobile systems. Yet temporal modeling approaches currently available tend to demand substantial computational resources or intricate parameter tuning, which meaningfully constrains their adoption on resource-limited edge devices. To address this gap, we introduce Temporal Naive Bayes (TNB), a lightweight and highly interpretable extension of the classical Naive Bayes classifier, developed specifically for sequential sensor data. TNB embeds a first-order autoregressive process directly into the feature likelihood estimation, thereby capturing temporal dependencies while incurring minimal computational overhead. The approach is validated across four scenarios of increasing complexity—from idealized synthetic data through to real-time deployment in the CARLA simulator and a real-world smartphone inertial measurement unit (IMU) dataset. Across these settings, TNB proves effective at isolating critical temporal dynamics, outperforming standard baselines in both multiclass maneuver recognition and anomaly detection tasks. An open-source pipeline accompanies this work, illustrating TNB’s practical value as a lightweight, real-time diagnostic tool for autonomous navigation.

title: A Reality Check of Inference-Time Context Augmentation Methods
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often fail to utilise the context given in the input, resulting in hallucinations or a fallback to parametric knowledge. Context augmentation methods aim to improve model performance by modifying the input, from inserting filler tokens that add computational time to adding relevant content such as elaboration of a context during inference. However, these methods have been evaluated in isolation and only by their performance gains, leaving it unclear how they compare and whether they reliably improve performance. In this paper, we present an evaluation framework spanning five methods that differ in how informative the inserted content is and apply them at the sentence level across seven models spanning multiple sizes on three datasets. We find that accuracy gains are not always genuine improvements but undirected perturbations: the methods correct some predictions while breaking others, particularly when the inserted text allows only for more computational time. Our analysis reveals that methods that bring no additional content primarily change model predictions near the decision boundary. Our findings highlight the need to evaluate the reliability of the accuracy gains before adopting them in practice.

title: Personalization, Prediction, and Persuasion
abstract: This chapter discusses the combination of personalization, prediction, and persuasion into a unified system of AI-based child-centric marketing. Its fundamental aspect is the so-called personalized persuasion that automatizes psychological profiling, predictive future behaviours, and persuasive design to create cognitive and emotional reactions. Through synthesis of the literature we discuss how the AI technology uses digital exhaust or traces left by children using educational apps, games and social media to form highly personalized experiences that are at the level of the child developmental stage. On the methodological level, the research investigates the technical processes underlying such tactics by integrating the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) with machine-learning algorithms like Gradient Boosting and the Random Forest to forecast the purchase intentions. This roadmap is part of the theoretical reflection and practical guide to researchers, marketers, and policymakers interested in knowing how an AI-based marketing ecosystem of the next generation will appear.

title: RheOPT: Few-Shot Non-Newtonian Flow Prediction via Newtonian Pretraining of RheOFormer
abstract: Despite advances in numerical methods, non-Newtonian flow simulations remain computationally expensive because velocity and stress must be advanced together through rate- and history-dependent constitutive dynamics. Neural-operator surrogates reduce inference cost after training, but their training data require the same expensive simulations they aim to replace, making data-efficient learning essential when only a few non-Newtonian simulations can be afforded. Here, we introduce the Rheological Operator Pretrained Transformer (RheOPT), which pretrains a transformer-based neural operator on inexpensive Newtonian simulations and fine-tunes it on a small number of non-Newtonian samples. Rather than transferring the Newtonian constitutive response itself, RheOPT reuses geometry-conditioned transport structure that remains useful after the stress model changes. We evaluate RheOPT in two geometry-matched settings: a $4{:}1$ contraction channel for Giesekus, Oldroyd-B, and Bingham fluids, and the oscillatory wake behind a triangular obstacle for Oldroyd-B flow. In the contraction, Newtonian pretraining substantially improves few-shot prediction, and a model fine-tuned on four target samples can match or exceed a from-scratch model trained on four times as many. This benefit is reliable under reversible instance normalization (RevIN) but dataset dependent under Global normalization, a difference we trace to the dynamic range of each fluid's velocity and stress fields. In the wake, where relative $L_2$ error alone cannot verify that vortex shedding is recovered, phase-insensitive diagnostics show that pretraining recovers the shedding frequency and wake fluctuation amplitude that are suppressed by the from-scratch model in the few-shot regime. Overall, RheOPT establishes Newtonian simulation as a physically grounded pretraining source for data-efficient non-Newtonian operator learning.

title: Diagnostic Loss: Asymmetric Supervision for Radiology Report Generation
abstract: Automated radiology report generation requires models to do more than produce fluent clinical narratives: they must explicitly state supported diagnoses while avoiding unsupported ones. However, existing medical vision-language models (MedVLMs) are typically trained with token-level maximum likelihood objectives, which prioritize text agreement over diagnostically critical terms. As a result, models can miss key diagnoses and introduce wrong ones. We identify this as an objective misalignment between conventional language modeling and the asymmetric diagnostic requirements of radiology reporting. To encode these requirements, we introduce Diagnostic Loss (DLoss), a differentiable, architecture-agnostic objective that operates directly on decoder token probabilities. DLoss separately aggregates probability mass over vocabularies associated with diagnoses supported by the reference report and with unsupported alternatives. Using asymmetric pooling across token positions in the report, it encourages supported diagnoses to receive sufficient probability in at least one position while suppressing spurious probability spikes for unsupported diagnoses across all positions during training. The loss can be applied to existing 3D MedVLMs without modifying their vision backbones, language decoders, or inference procedures, and introduces no additional inference-time computation. We train and evaluate DLoss on 50,000 abdominal CT scans across several 3D MedVLM architectures on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution report-generation benchmarks. evidence.title: Diagnostic Loss: Asymmetric Supervision for Radiology Report Generation
evidence.abstract: Automated radiology report generation requires models to do more than produce fluent clinical narratives: they must explicitly state supported diagnoses while avoiding unsupported ones. However, existing medical vision-language models (MedVLMs) are typically trained with token-level maximum likelihood objectives, which prioritize text agreement over diagnostically critical terms. As a result, models can miss key diagnoses and introduce wrong ones. We identify this as an objective misalignment between conventional language modeling and the asymmetric diagnostic requirements of radiology reporting. To encode these requirements, we introduce Diagnostic Loss (DLoss), a differentiable, architecture-agnostic objective that operates directly on decoder token probabilities. DLoss separately aggregates probability mass over vocabularies associated with diagnoses supported by the reference report and with unsupported alternatives. Using asymmetric pooling across token positions in the report, it encourages supported diagnoses to receive sufficient probability in at least one position while suppressing spurious probability spikes for unsupported diagnoses across all positions during training. The loss can be applied to existing 3D MedVLMs without modifying their vision backbones, language decoders, or inference procedures, and introduces no additional inference-time computation. title: Clinical Artificial Intelligence in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: From Early Detection and Computational Pathology to Precision Oncology
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being developed to analyze radiological, histopathological, molecular, and clinical data across the non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) pathway. This narrative review examines representative applications through August 2026, focusing on intended clinical use, validation, and the evidence required to influence care. Studies were selected purposively for clinical relevance and methodological importance. Imaging models support investigation of nodule detection, malignancy estimation, and future lung cancer risk, although predictive performance does not establish the benefit of changing screening or diagnostic pathways. In computational pathology, models classify tissue, quantify morphological features, and estimate selected molecular alterations. Foundation models extend these capabilities, but their evaluation requires attention to pretraining provenance and independence of downstream testing. Histology-based molecular prediction does not currently justify replacing validated molecular assays; prioritization of testing requires prospective workflow evaluation. Models evaluated in immunotherapy-treated cohorts can predict response or survival, but these associations do not establish differential benefit between treatments. The principal limitations include selected retrospective populations, incomplete assessment of calibration and clinically relevant thresholds, uncertain transportability, and limited evaluation of model-guided care. Evidence should therefore be interpreted at the level of the individual system and intended decision. Prospective evaluation, appropriate comparators, explicit failure procedures, and post-deployment monitoring are required before technical performance can be translated into clinical benefit.

title: Adaptive Skill Granularity for Coding Agents: Runtime Routing and Macro-to-Micro Recovery
abstract: Reusable skills allow large language model agents to package task-specific procedures, tool affordances, and execution guidance into modular units. Prior work has largely studied how agents retrieve, compose, or synthesize skills before execution. In coding agents, however, execution poses an additional runtime control problem: the same task may be solved through primitive tool calls, macro skills, or hybrid execution that starts with a macro and falls back to micro-level recovery. We introduce Adaptive Skill Granularity, a framework that treats skill granularity as an action-abstraction policy conditioned on task structure, execution state, and macro-skill failures. The system combines a feature-based granularity controller and a finite-state recovery executor. We evaluate the framework with a deterministic coding-agent protocol using verifier-defined success, total cost, and process metrics such as macro adoption, failure recovery, route match, and transition correctness. Results show that fixed macro execution is efficient when applicable but brittle under mismatch, while runtime routing and explicit macro-to-micro recovery improve robustness and recover controlled macro failures that fixed-granularity execution leaves unresolved. Our findings suggest that skill libraries for coding agents should be treated not only as retrievable resources, but also as controllable, verifiable, and recoverable execution abstractions.

title: LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications
abstract: Vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication enables connected vehicles to make safety-critical decisions, but delayed, missing, or incorrect information can compromise driving safety. Systematically testing such failures is challenging because traffic interactions, communication conditions, and application responses must be jointly configured to produce meaningful scenarios. This paper presents LAST-V2X, a language-driven, adaptive framework for automated scenario synthesis and safety testing of V2X applications. LAST-V2X leverages large language models (LLMs) to translate natural-language test descriptions into executable scenarios grounded in roadway geometry, V2X communication semantics, and vehicle behavior. The framework integrates physical traffic simulation with spatially aware communication modeling and message-level fault injection to evaluate how information degradation affects vehicle decisions. To establish whether an observed safety failure is caused by communication rather than the underlying traffic conditions, LAST-V2X employs matched executions under degraded and ground-truth information. Furthermore, an execution-guided refinement mechanism combines parameter search and LLM self-reflection to identify ineffective test configurations, improve scenario effectiveness, and produce minimal reproducible failure cases. Experiments across diverse CARLA environments and V2X safety applications demonstrate the framework's ability to generate reliable scenarios, distinguish communication-induced failures from unrelated safety violations, and substantially improve failure discovery through adaptive refinement. These results establish LAST-V2X as a systematic approach to language-driven, causally verified, and adaptive safety testing for connected vehicle systems.

title: Bidirectional Path Integral Monte Carlo Simulation of Quantum Circuits
abstract: We propose an approximate classical algorithm for estimating quantum circuits' transition amplitudes, $\langle Ψ_f | \hat{U} | Ψ_0 \rangle$, based on Monte Carlo sums over bidirectionally sampled Feynman paths. The algorithm generates Feynman paths, i.e., sequences of intermediate computational basis states, by combining information from random walks initiated at both the input and output states, $Ψ_0$ and $Ψ_f$, respectively. It further combines this bidirectional approach with Multiple Importance Sampling, a powerful variance reduction technique that avoids variance peaks caused by divisions by the very low sampling probabilities associated with hard to reach paths. Empirical data demonstrate the superior convergence rate exhibited by the bidirectional algorithm over a unidirectional, forward-only sampling approach. This superiority is due to the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm in finding and weighting paths with non-zero amplitude in an extremely sparse path space. Sum of paths algorithms exhibit very favourable space complexity. Monte Carlo replaces exhaustive enumeration of the exponentially large path space by stochastic sampling, the computational cost being determined by the variance of the estimator. This work demonstrates these two features by presenting results on very large quantum circuits, with up to 4096 qubits.

title: How Different, or Different How? Stance Granularity in Viewpoint Selection for Dialog Systems that Engage Users with Alternative Views
abstract: Systems that aim to help a user engage with viewpoints other than their own have to decide how different those viewpoints should be. Viewpoints are mainly represented on a scalar scale, too coarse to distinguish viewpoints that disagree with the user about different things. We introduce a selection policy in which a bandit sets how far viewpoints may sit from the user, and the policy selects the most novel viewpoint within that bound. We vary only its stance encoder, comparing a scalar score with Perspectivized Stance Vectors, which break a position into separate stances on concepts. We integrate it inside a dialog system and run a between-subjects study (N=63). Concept-level stance produces more varied exposure sequences and broader coverage of the topic's positions, but does not change how deeply users justify viewpoints or how accurately they reconstruct them. Finally, we analyze user--viewpoint relations at the concept level, showing that users reconstruct a viewpoint least accurately on concepts that one side took no position on, rather than on concepts where the two disagreed. Our findings open up opportunities for dialog systems that support engagement with alternative viewpoints by acting on which concepts a user and a viewpoint disagree on, rather than on distance alone.

title: GraphCAD: Geometry-Aware Diffusion on Edge-Adjacency Graphs for CAD Generation
abstract: Generative modeling for Computer-Aided Design (CAD) remains fundamentally challenged by the need to capture the intricate interplay between discrete topological connectivity and precise spatial geometry inherent in Boundary Representations (B-reps). Existing generative approaches largely formulate CAD construction as a sequence modeling problem, but consequently lack an explicit topological inductive bias. In this work, we present GraphCAD, a geometry-aware generative framework that centers modeling on the Edge-Adjacency Graph (EAG), a novel graph-based CAD representation tailored for generative tasks. GraphCAD adopts a hybrid graph diffusion formulation to jointly model the discrete and continuous components of EAG and introduces a geometry-aware denoising mechanism that renders node attributes into spatial point sets. These point sets are encoded by an SE(3)-equivariant backbone and fused into the node representations, thereby grounding the generative process in physical geometry. To support this study, we construct EAGBench, a large-scale dataset of engineering CAD models. Extensive experiments show that GraphCAD can generate complex CAD models with more than 50 faces and achieves state-of-the-art performance in geometric fidelity and distributional alignment compared with sequence-based baselines.

title: The Invisible Handshake
abstract: This chapter aims to examine the role played by artificial intelligence in determining the consumer behaviors and buying patterns of children in a digital environment. The chapter focuses on the mechanisms employed by artificial intelligence in marketing, which include collecting consumer data, tracking consumer behavior, persuasion architecture, artificial influencers, hyper-personalization, the Internet of Toys, and voice assistants. The chapter is also concerned with the psychological and emotional triggers employed by artificial intelligence in marketing to consumers, which include fear of missing out, gamification, and reward-based engagement systems. The chapter is concerned with the ethical issues associated with artificial intelligence marketing to consumers, which include issues related to consumer data privacy, manipulation, transparency, and the lack of regulations. The chapter is also concerned with emerging trends in artificial intelligence marketing to consumers, which include considerations related to marketing ethics

title: Synthesis of Reliable Logic Question Answering Data for Large Language Model with Aid of Operations Research Program
abstract: Logical reasoning is a highly valued capability in language models. However, high-quality logical reasoning data remain scarce, while manual data creation is costly and time-consuming. We introduce Operations Research Aided Synthesis (ORAS), a solver-verified, two-layer incremental framework for synthesizing logic question-answering data. ORAS leverages operations research techniques to systematically generate high-quality datasets for evaluating large language models (LLMs) and, when used for training, improving their reasoning capabilities. ORAS's pipeline integrates mathematical programming methods to generate question-answer pairs, and then employs a dual-phase approach: the first phase uses optimization algorithms to construct and evaluate the logic systems by solving the problem using a mathematical solver. The second phase translates the logic system to human-readable problems and generates answers according to the information from the mathematical solver. The fine-tuned model achieves a 22%-33% (percentage point) improvement in accuracy on in-sample tests and a 4%-22% (percentage point) improvement on similar out-of-sample tests.

title: MixPT: Point Transformer with Interleaved Window and Global Attention
abstract: Point cloud transformers aim to capture detailed local geometry and relationships across a scene at a manageable computational cost. Two common approaches are window attention and global attention. They differ in how they enable scene-wide interaction, which refers to information exchange among tokens across a scene. Window attention reduces computational cost by restricting self-attention to groups of tokens called windows; in serialized designs, each window contains a fixed number of consecutive tokens from a spatially ordered sequence. Because each block only directly connects tokens within the same window, information exchange across windows relies on changes in window membership across blocks and hierarchical pooling. Global attention, in contrast, directly connects all tokens within a scene, but computing attention over all token pairs can be costly when the number of tokens is large. To balance computational cost and scene-wide interaction, we introduce MixPT, a point transformer that uses a mix of window and global attention blocks in an interleaved schedule, while retaining a single fixed serialization pattern for its window blocks. For scenes with a large number of tokens, MixPT applies global attention to spatially pooled tokens and returns residual updates to the original-resolution stream. Across indoor and outdoor benchmarks, MixPT achieves competitive accuracy with lower latency than representative window and global attention baselines. We further demonstrate the feasibility of scaling the attention stage in depth by repeating the interleaved pattern of window and global attention blocks.

title: Zero-Shot Forecasting of In-Situ Soil Moisture and Temperature with a Time-Series Foundation Model
abstract: Soil moisture and temperature govern plant-water availability and microbial activity, making them key indicators for evaluating land-restoration efforts on degraded landscapes. However, the physical and data-driven models normally used to forecast them both need information that a newly instrumented restoration site does not yet have: hydraulic parameters for the former and months of per-site training data for the latter. We evaluate TimesFM 1, a 500M-parameter time-series foundation model, zero-shot on 15-minute telemetry from 27 sensor stations across three land-management regimes (Control, Treatment, Scald) at a semi-arid restoration site, forecasting 5 cm and 30 cm soil moisture and enclosure temperature at seven lead times from 1 h to 168 h. Using gap-aware rolling-origin evaluation across sensors, we find that TimesFM beats the best rule-based statistical forecasting baselines (persistence, seasonal-naive, or 7-day climatology) by 21-76% at sub-daily lead times but loses by 6-79% beyond a day, a pattern explained by a diurnal-alignment mechanism that holds for both soil-moisture depths and temperature. A CatBoost baseline trained walk-forward on the same origins with full history and weather covariates never wins overall, and we show that its weakness is partly a cold-start effect specific to short deployments. We additionally quantify the inference cost of zero-shot forecasting on commodity CPU hardware. Our results highlight a practical trade-off between zero-shot forecasting capability, predictive performance, and computational efficiency.

title: Lasagna: a compositional framework for RAG component evaluation
abstract: Lasagna isolates the stages of a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline behind typed contracts so that a single component can be replaced while everything else is held fixed, making a measured difference attributable to the change. It ships benchmark adapters, retrieval and generation metrics, paired significance testing, and a results format carrying the provenance needed to compare runs between machines.

title: Quantum Entanglement Generation and Finite-Range Spin Coupling: A Three-Axis Null Test in a Physical-Observation Dual-Axis Model
abstract: We study the generation of quantum entanglement between two spatially separated spins and propose a two-ion experiment to test a finite-range interaction. In a specified quantum realization of the physical–observation dual-axis (PODA) model, a low-energy expansion of a local matter–field action yields a curl-type spin source. Eliminating the quantized field modes to second order produces a cross interaction containing products of the two endpoint spin operators. We derive the resulting entanglement dynamics from an initial product state and give a measurement-based witness applicable to noisy mixed states. For one static bridge-field channel in an unbounded homogeneous background, the trace of the coupling tensor contains a nonzero contribution set by the response length. The corresponding trace vanishes for the free-space, noncontact, quasistatic magnetic dipole interaction. With finite-source contact terms retained, this distinction leads to a direct estimator: the sum of the signed exchange coefficients measured along three common orthogonal quantization axes equals the trace of the same physical coupling tensor.The proposed trapped-ion protocol specifies phase readout, a distance scan, interleaved axis settings, error calibration, and a likelihood for the raw joint counts. Entanglement certification and interaction testing are separate inferences, based on state records and the tensor trace, respectively. We examine angular errors, motion-mediated coupling, boundaries, secular reduction, and readout dynamics, and calculate the sensitivity and acquisition time for five micrometre-scale separations. An unknown constant offset and a residual inverse-cube background substantially weaken the expected constraints. The model, assumptions, derivations, and statistical criteria are given within the paper. The numerical results are conditional design forecasts, not new measurements. Converting a measured interval into constraints on PODA action parameters requires independent matching to the experimental matter and the selected field channel.

title: Multi-Token Prediction and Alternative Tokenization Improve Learning Latent Multi-Hop Graph Search at Scale
abstract: Given an unseen graph, a start node, $s$, and an end node, $t$, can a language model generate the shortest path from $s$ to $t$? Prior work has found that models fail to learn this task as the graphs scale. We show that this failure has two causes: the supervision signal and the tokenization. First, we theoretically establish and empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of multi-token prediction (MTP), and show that the benefits of MTP are topologically agnostic. Second, we introduce alternative tokenizations and show that the two causes are orthogonal. Using these methods, we break through the scaling wall observed by prior work, consistently and stably learning to solve the task at scales far beyond previous limits.

title: From Data-Driven to Geology-Informed Learning: Geometry-Aware Graph Transformer Learning for Geo-Energy Systems
abstract: Geo-energy systems involve heterogeneous subsurface properties, irregular spatial structures, and complex interactions. Conventional data-driven models either treat observations independently or rely on graph connectivity without explicitly encoding relative geometry, which limits their ability to distinguish spatially different configurations. This study develops a Geometry-Aware Graph Transformer (GAGT) that integrates node attributes, graph structure, and relative geometric information through a learnable geometric bias in the attention mechanism. A controlled synthetic experiment with 300 irregularly distributed three-dimensional nodes compares a multilayer perceptron (MLP), a Graph Transformer (GT), and GAGT under identical settings. Across 10 random seeds, GAGT achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.1569, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.2152, and a coefficient of determination ($R^2$) of 0.8678, reducing MAE and RMSE by 35.77% and 33.95%, respectively, relative to GT. In this controlled setting, explicit geometry therefore carries predictive information that graph connectivity alone does not provide. GAGT can serve as a geometry-aware representation layer between purely data-driven learning and more comprehensive geology-informed modeling; validation with real geological data and physically constrained simulations is still required.

title: DIAL: Steerable Language Models with Distilled Instruction-Adherence Levels
abstract: When a user says "Keep it short", how short should the LLM's response be? More generally, users and applications require different levels of instruction adherence, but prompting does not reliably provide fine-grained control over them. We therefore study "steerable language models" that provide fine-grained numerical control over the degree to which models follow general instructions specified in text. However, existing approaches do not jointly offer fine-grained control, efficiency, and scalability across diverse instructions. To address this gap, we introduce DIAL (Distilled Instruction-Adherence Levels) to achieve all three properties. For fine-grained control, we perform classifier-free guidance (CFG) with a frozen LLM to provide training signals for on-policy distillation of instruction adherence at different levels. For efficiency, we design a lightweight steering adapter that uses a classifier over the LLM's hidden states to compute a closed-form steering edit. The classifier adaptively sets the steering magnitude at each token based on the target adherence level, while accounting for the geometry of the LLM's hidden states to preserve response coherence. For scalability, the classifier is text-conditioned, allowing a shared adapter to support new instructions without per-instruction fitting, and training requires only instruction and request text. Evaluation across multiple LLM families shows that DIAL achieves a competitive balance between concept expression and response fluency, with concept scores increasing monotonically across adherence levels. We introduce SteerIF, an instruction-only dataset of 98, 625 concept, persona, verifiable, and descriptive instructions. When trained on SteerIF, DIAL provides fine-grained control over personas and, when combined with prompting, improves verifiable instruction following.

title: Bound-Conditioned Latent Inference for Progressive Image Compression
abstract: Progressive image compression reconstructs images from prefixes of a single bitstream and therefore involves sequential latent inference under partial observations. Existing trit-plane codecs mainly treat decoded trits as discrete symbols for probability prediction, without fully exploiting their role as interval constraints on the underlying continuous latents. We propose bound-conditioned latent inference (BLI), a framework that reformulates progressive trit-plane coding as sequential latent inference under shrinking interval constraints. At each coding step, the trits decoded so far define lower and upper bounds for each latent element. BLI uses the center and width of these bounds, together with hyperprior information shared by the encoder and decoder, to jointly refine the Gaussian parameters $(μ,σ)$ for entropy modeling and the latent estimate $\hat{y}$ for reconstruction. As additional trits are decoded, the feasible intervals shrink monotonically, yielding tighter constraints for the next inference step and enabling flexible in-plane refinement schedules. Experiments on Kodak, CLIC, and JPEG-AI show that BLI achieves state-of-the-art rate-distortion performance among progressive image codecs, reducing BD-rate by $17.78\%$ over DPICT and by $7.96\%$ over CTC on Kodak, while replacing CTC's plane-specific predictors with a shared model that uses about $5.3\times$ fewer parameters and achieves lower latency than CTC.

title: A clinically conditional deep learning model for predicting histological subtypes of pituitary neuroendocrine tumors from hematoxylin-eosin whole-slide images
abstract: Histological subtype classification of pituitary neuroendocrine tumors is important for prognostic assessment and therapeutic decision-making. However, current subtype classification relies heavily on extensive immunohistochemistry, which can be time-consuming, costly, and tissue-consuming. We aimed to develop a clinically conditional deep learning model that integrates routinely available clinical features with hematoxylin-eosin-stained whole-slide images to predict five subtypes of pituitary neuroendocrine tumors. To address the histomorphologic characteristics of pituitary neuroendocrine tumors, we designed an automatic pathology-informed patch selection strategy focusing on diagnostically relevant tumor regions, and applied a masking strategy to simulate missing clinical features. Model performance was evaluated using ensemble inference from five cross-validated models on an internal test set and a temporal and external validation set. Models were assessed by accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, with 95% confidence intervals. Paired DeLong and McNemar tests were used to compare models, with P < 0.05 considered significant. Attention heatmaps were visualized for interpretability. On the internal hold-out test set, the clinically conditional model achieved an overall accuracy of 91.8% and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.934, outperforming the unimodal WSIs model (accuracy, 87.3%; AUC, 0.905; P < 0.05). On the temporal and external validation set, the clinically conditional model achieved an overall accuracy of 86.9% and an AUC of 0.901, also surpassing the unimodal model based only on WSIs (accuracy, 84.6%; AUC, 0.868; P < 0.05). Interpretability analyses showed that model attention was concentrated in morphologically meaningful regions and that the decision process was similar to recognized pathological features of individual PitNETs subtypes. These preliminary findings suggest that integrating clinical feature with histopathology may better simulate the comprehensive reasoning process of pathologists in routine diagnoses. This exploratory approach could potentially serve as a supplementary decision-support tool to facilitate ancillary test prioritization, optimize diagnostic workflow, and improve resource allocation, particularly in resource-constrained settings.

title: An Integrative Approach for Subtyping Mental Disorders Using Multimodal Data
abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding the biological and behavioral heterogeneity underlying psychiatric disorders is critical for advancing precision diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. This paper addresses the scientific question of how multimodal data, which spans clinical, cognitive, and neuroimaging measures, can be integrated to identify biologically meaningful subtypes of mental disorders. We introduce Mixed INtegrative Data Subtyping (MINDS), a Bayesian hierarchical model designed to jointly analyze mixed‐type data for simultaneous dimension reduction and clustering. Using data from the adolescent brain cognitive development (ABCD) Study, MINDS integrates clinical symptoms, cognitive performance, and brain structure measures to subtype attention‐deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and obsessive‐compulsive disorder (OCD). Our method leverages Pólya–Gamma augmentation for computational efficiency and robust inference. Simulations demonstrate improved stability and accuracy compared to existing clustering approaches. Application to the ABCD data reveals clinically interpretable subtypes of ADHD and OCD with distinct cognitive and neurodevelopmental profiles. These findings show how integrative multimodal modeling can enhance the reproducibility and clinical relevance of psychiatric subtyping, funding data‐driven policies for early identification and targeted interventions in mental health.
